---
title: "Network Meta-Analysis: Models and Identifiability"
---

## Introduction {#sec-nma-intro}

The previous chapter built an indirect comparison from a single triangle: a study of $A$ against a
common comparator $C$, a study of $B$ against the same $C$, and the subtraction
$\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}$ that the algebra of contrasts licenses under transitivity
(@thm-bucher-unbiased). A health technology assessment is rarely so tidy. It must usually weigh a dozen
treatments compared in a scatter of trials, some two-armed and some multi-armed, some sharing comparators
and some not, with the same pairwise contrast occasionally informed by both a direct head-to-head trial
and one or more indirect paths. **Network meta-analysis** (NMA) is the apparatus that pools all of this
evidence at once into a single coherent set of relative effects, estimating every pairwise contrast in
the network, including contrasts never studied head to head, while honoring the correlations that
multi-arm trials and shared comparators impose.

Why pool everything into one model instead of running a separate Bucher comparison for each pair of
treatments? Three reasons, each made precise in this chapter. First, pooling *borrows strength*: a
contrast with no direct head-to-head trial is still estimated, informed by every indirect path through
the network, and a contrast carrying both direct and indirect evidence combines the two efficiently
rather than discarding either. Second, pooling *respects structure*: a three-arm trial is one randomized
experiment, not three independent two-arm trials, and a single model preserves the correlations that such
shared-comparator designs impose, correlations that separate pairwise calculations would silently throw
away. Third, pooling *makes coherence testable*: isolated pairwise comparisons cannot notice that the
whole web of relative effects must fit together, whereas the network can check whether the direct and
indirect routes to a contrast agree, and flag them when they do not. Chapter 14 gave the single triangle;
this chapter gives the whole web, together with the tools to decide which of its contrasts a reader may
trust.

This chapter develops the standard NMA model as a piece of mathematics. The organizing idea is that an
NMA is a generalized linear model (@def-glm): each trial arm contributes one observation, the link-scale
arm means are a linear function $\boldsymbol\theta=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta$ of a parameter vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ through a design matrix $\mathbf X$, and the entire analytic content of the method,
its estimability and its assumptions, is read off from the structure of $\mathbf X$. Bucher's estimator
is then visible as the special case in which $\mathbf X$ encodes one triangle and two studies, and the
question "which contrasts can the network estimate?" becomes the linear-algebra question "which columns
of $\mathbf X$ are independent?"

We prove, in full, the results that make this picture rigorous. We give the two standard
parameterizations of the arm means, the **baseline-shift** form (@def-baseline-shift-param) that names a
separate contrast inside each study and the **reference-treatment** form (@def-reference-treatment-param)
that names a single network-wide contrast per treatment, and we prove they describe the same model
exactly on the subspace where the consistency equations hold (@thm-parameterization-equivalence). We
prove that the network contrasts are identifiable if and only if the treatment graph is connected, by
computing the rank of the design matrix through the rank of a graph incidence matrix
(@thm-fe-nma-identifiability). We derive the characteristic one-half correlation between two contrasts
that share an arm in a multi-arm trial, and we show that the one-half is not an arbitrary modeling choice
but the unique value that makes the heterogeneity variance independent of which arm is called the
baseline (@thm-re-nma-correlation). We prove the algebraic closure of the consistency equations
(@thm-consistency-closure), which says that the $\binom{K}{2}$ pairwise contrasts of a $K$-treatment
network are generated by $K-1$ basis contrasts and constrained by exactly $\binom{K-1}{2}$ loop
identities, the very identities that node-splitting (@def-node-splitting) tests for inconsistency. We
extend the model to individual patient data and prove the identifiability of the network meta-regression
(@thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability), the springboard for the population-adjustment methods of Parts IV and V.
We close the theory with the goodness-of-fit machinery the applied literature reports for these models,
the residual deviance (@def-residual-deviance) and the deviance information criterion (@def-dic). A fully
worked triangle-plus-extra-arm network, carried from a design matrix to fitted contrasts, standard
errors, a node-split, and a residual deviance, makes every formula concrete.

Throughout we use the notation of [Notation](/notation.qmd): $j$ indexes studies, $k$ indexes treatments
and arms, $\theta_{jk}$ is the link-scale mean of arm $k$ in study $j$, $\mu_j$ is a study baseline,
$d_{ab}$ is the network contrast of treatment $b$ versus treatment $a$, and $\delta_{j,\,t_1 t_k}$ is a
study-level contrast. The chapter corresponds to results D.5 through D.14 of the proof catalogue in
`proofs/D_network_meta_analysis.md`, and it builds directly on the Bucher development of Chapter 14
(@def-transitivity, @def-constancy-relative-effects, @thm-bucher-unbiased, @thm-bucher-variance) and the
pairwise meta-analysis of Chapter 13 (@thm-fixed-effect-blue, @thm-dersimonian-laird, @def-i-squared).

## A running example and a reader's toolkit {#sec-nma-running}

The formal development below moves quickly into design matrices, graphs, and rank conditions. To keep it
anchored, we fix one small clinical network now and carry it through every section. A reader who holds
this picture in mind can translate each abstract step back into trials and drugs.

::: {#exm-nma-running}
## Three treatments, four trials
A health technology assessment compares three treatments for a single condition:

- treatment $1$ = **placebo** (the network reference),
- treatment $2$ = **Drug A**,
- treatment $3$ = **Drug B**.

Four randomized trials are available. Each reports a relative effect on the log-odds scale (a log odds
ratio); a positive value means the second-named treatment raises the odds of a good outcome.

| Study $j$ | Arms | Design | Comparison(s) it reports |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | placebo, Drug A | two-arm | Drug A vs placebo |
| 2 | placebo, Drug B | two-arm | Drug B vs placebo |
| 3 | Drug A, Drug B | two-arm (head-to-head) | Drug B vs Drug A |
| 4 | placebo, Drug A, Drug B | three-arm | Drug A vs placebo, and Drug B vs placebo |

Drawing a dot for each treatment and a line for each within-study comparison gives the
**treatment-comparison graph**:

```
                  (2) Drug A
                  /         \
       studies 1, 4          study 3
                /             \
   (1) placebo  --------------  (3) Drug B
                studies 2, 4
```

Three facts can be read straight off the picture, and the rest of the chapter turns each one into a
theorem.

- **Direct versus indirect evidence.** Every pair is compared directly by at least one trial: placebo vs
Drug A (studies 1 and 4), placebo vs Drug B (studies 2 and 4), Drug A vs Drug B (study 3). Drug A vs
Drug B is *also* estimable indirectly, by chaining Drug A vs placebo with placebo vs Drug B.
- **Connectedness.** One can travel from any treatment to any other along the lines. This is what lets the
network estimate every relative effect, including ones with no direct trial; @thm-fe-nma-identifiability
makes it precise.
- **A loop.** The three edges $1$-$2$, $2$-$3$, $1$-$3$ close a triangle. That loop is what makes it
possible to *test* whether the direct and indirect routes to Drug A vs Drug B agree;
@thm-consistency-closure and @sec-nma-nodesplit build the test. A tree-shaped network with no loop offers
nothing to test.

Study $4$, the three-arm trial, is the source of most of the subtlety in this chapter. Its full numerical
analysis is completed in @exm-nma-triangle. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The picture uses standard graph words. Here is the whole vocabulary in trial language; keep it nearby.

| Graph term | What it means for the evidence |
|---|---|
| vertex (node) | a treatment |
| edge | one within-study comparison (a single randomized contrast) |
| path | a chain of comparisons linking two treatments |
| connected | every treatment is reachable from every other by comparisons |
| connected component | a maximal cluster of treatments joined by comparisons |
| loop (cycle) | a closed chain: both a direct and an indirect route between two treatments |
| direct evidence (on $a$ vs $b$) | a trial that randomized patients between $a$ and $b$ |
| indirect evidence (on $a$ vs $b$) | an estimate of $a$ vs $b$ obtained through a path via other treatments |

Four quantities recur throughout, and beginners routinely blend them. The next table previews them with
plain meanings and a running-example instance; the precise definitions follow in @sec-nma-glm and
@sec-nma-param, so nothing here is used before it is defined later.

| Symbol | Plain-language meaning | In the running example |
|---|---|---|
| $\theta_{jk}$ | outcome *level* of arm $k$ in study $j$, on the link scale | log-odds of a good outcome on the Drug A arm of study $1$ |
| $\mu_j$ | study $j$ baseline: its reference arm's level | log-odds on the placebo arm of study $1$ |
| $\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}$ | a *study-specific* contrast: treatment $k$ vs that study's own baseline arm | Drug A vs placebo as measured inside study $1$ |
| $d_k$ | the *network-wide* contrast of treatment $k$ vs the reference $1$ (one number for the whole network) | Drug A vs placebo, pooled across all trials |
| $d_{ab}=d_b-d_a$ | the network contrast of treatment $b$ vs treatment $a$, recovered by subtraction | Drug B vs Drug A, pooled |
| $t_{j,1}$ | the arm chosen as study $j$'s baseline | placebo, in study $1$ |
| $\tilde{\mathbf d}=(d_1,\dots,d_K)$ | the network contrasts padded with $d_1=0$ (length $K$); the unpadded $\mathbf d=(d_2,\dots,d_K)$ has length $K-1$ | $\tilde{\mathbf d}=(0,d_2,d_3)$ |

The single most common conceptual slip is to confuse a study-specific contrast $\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}$
(one study's answer) with a network contrast $d_k$ or $d_{ab}$ (the pooled answer). The whole point of an
NMA is to build the network contrasts out of the study-specific ones.

::: {.remark}
**Reading the sign of a contrast.** The convention $d_{ab}=d_b-d_a$ means "treatment $b$ versus treatment
$a$", with $b$ in the favored-if-positive direction. On the logit scale a contrast is a log odds ratio:
$d_{ab}>0$ says $b$ raises the odds of the outcome relative to $a$, and the odds ratio is
$\mathrm{OR}_{ab}=e^{d_{ab}}$. Reversing the order flips the sign and inverts the odds ratio:
$d_{ba}=-d_{ab}$ and $\mathrm{OR}_{ba}=1/\mathrm{OR}_{ab}$. For instance a log-odds contrast of $0.5$ is an
odds ratio $e^{0.5}\approx1.65$; the same comparison written the other way is $-0.5$, an odds ratio
$e^{-0.5}\approx0.61$. Applied papers are inconsistent about direction, so always check which treatment is
named first. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The network as a generalized linear model {#sec-nma-glm}

A network of evidence is a finite collection of randomized studies. Study $j\in\{1,\dots,J\}$ randomizes
patients among a set of arms $\mathcal A_j\subseteq\{1,\dots,K\}$, where $\{1,\dots,K\}$ enumerates the
treatments under comparison and treatment $1$ is a fixed network reference (often placebo or standard of
care). We write $A_j=|\mathcal A_j|\ge 2$ for the number of arms in study $j$, and we designate one arm
$t_{j,1}\in\mathcal A_j$ as the study baseline; nothing of substance depends on which arm is chosen as
$t_{j,1}$, a freedom we exploit in @sec-nma-equivalence. The total number of arms in the network is
$$
N \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{J} A_j ,
$$ {#eq-nma-totalarms}
and the total number of within-study contrasts, one fewer than the arm count in each study, is
$$
C \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{J} (A_j-1) \;=\; N - J .
$$ {#eq-nma-totalcontrasts}

The treatments that are compared, directly or by sharing a trial, form a graph.

::: {#def-nma-arm-model}
## The arm-based network model
The **treatment-comparison graph** $G=(\mathcal V,\mathcal E)$ has vertex set $\mathcal V=\{1,\dots,K\}$,
one vertex per treatment, and one edge for each within-study contrast: study $j$ with baseline $t_{j,1}$
contributes the $A_j-1$ edges $\{t_{j,1},k\}$ for $k\in\mathcal A_j\setminus\{t_{j,1}\}$. Parallel edges
from different studies are kept distinct, so $G$ is in general a multigraph with $|\mathcal E|=C$ edges.

For a chosen link function $g$ (@def-link-function), let $\theta_{jk}=g(\bar\mu_{jk})$ be the link-scale
mean outcome of arm $k$ in study $j$, where $\bar\mu_{jk}$ is the marginal mean response in that arm. The
**arm-based network model** writes the vector $\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathbb R^{N}$ of all arm means as a
linear predictor
$$
\boldsymbol\theta \;=\; \mathbf X\,\boldsymbol\beta ,
$$ {#eq-nma-linpred}
for a design matrix $\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{N\times p}$ and a parameter vector $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb
R^{p}$. Coupled with a response distribution from an exponential family (@def-exponential-family), for
instance $r_{jk}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_{jk},g^{-1}(\theta_{jk}))$ for binary outcomes under the logit link,
@eq-nma-linpred makes the network a generalized linear model. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader's translation of the arm model.** Stack all the trial arms into one tall column
$\boldsymbol\theta$, one entry per arm. In the running example the arms are placebo and Drug A (study
$1$), placebo and Drug B (study $2$), Drug A and Drug B (study $3$), and placebo, Drug A, Drug B (study
$4$), so $\boldsymbol\theta$ has $N=9$ entries; for example $\theta_{4,2}$ is the log-odds of a good
outcome on the Drug A arm of the three-arm study $4$. The model @eq-nma-linpred says every one of these
arm levels is assembled from a handful of shared ingredients, the study baselines and the treatment
effects, through the table $\mathbf X$. The two appearances of the link, $\theta_{jk}=g(\bar\mu_{jk})$ in
the definition and $g^{-1}(\theta_{jk})$ in the binomial example, are the same map read in opposite
directions: $\theta$ is the arm's outcome level moved onto the additive scale where treatment effects add
up, and $g^{-1}$ moves it back to a probability. With the logit link, $\theta_{jk}=0.5$ corresponds to a
response probability $g^{-1}(0.5)=1/(1+e^{-0.5})\approx0.62$. The *treatment-comparison graph* is nothing
more than the picture of @exm-nma-running: a dot per treatment, a line per within-study comparison.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Multi-arm trials: clinical pairs versus contrast rows.** A three-arm trial such as study $4$ compares
all three treatment pairs within one randomized experiment, so clinically it carries direct evidence on
placebo vs Drug A, placebo vs Drug B, *and* Drug A vs Drug B. The graph definition, however, gives it only
$A_j-1=2$ edges: after we name one arm the study baseline (here placebo), we keep the $2$ contrasts *to
that baseline* and treat the third pairwise comparison, Drug A vs Drug B, as their difference. This is no
loss of information. The omitted contrast is recovered exactly by subtraction,
$\delta_{\text{A vs B}}=\delta_{\text{placebo vs B}}-\delta_{\text{placebo vs A}}$, and it is *correlated*
with the two kept contrasts because all three share the placebo arm. Keeping $A_j-1$ independent contrasts
rather than all $\binom{A_j}{2}$ pairwise comparisons is what keeps the rows of the design linearly
independent; carrying their correlation, computed in @thm-re-nma-correlation, is what keeps the standard
errors honest. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Equation @eq-nma-linpred is the entire formal commitment of an NMA: a single linear predictor across all
studies, tying the arms together through shared treatment parameters. Two specifications of
$(\mathbf X,\boldsymbol\beta)$ are in standard use, and the bulk of this chapter studies them and their
consequences. Before naming them we record the sense in which the chapter generalizes the last one.

::: {.remark}
**Bucher as a two-study, one-triangle network.** Recall the Bucher triangle of Chapter 14: two active
treatments each compared against a common comparator. Relabel that comparator as the network reference,
treatment $1$, and the two actives as treatments $2$ and $3$. With two two-arm studies, one on $\{1,2\}$
and one on $\{1,3\}$, we have $K=3$, $N=4$, $J=2$, and $C=(2-1)+(2-1)=2$ within-study contrasts; the graph
$G$ is the path $2-1-3$. The arm-based model has one baseline and one contrast per study, and eliminating
the two baselines leaves exactly the contrasts $d_{12}$ and $d_{13}$, whose difference
$d_{13}-d_{12}=d_{23}$ is the Bucher estimator (@thm-bucher-unbiased). The graph is connected but contains
no cycle, so there is direct evidence on $2$ versus $1$ and on $3$ versus $1$ but only indirect evidence
on $3$ versus $2$; there is nothing to test for inconsistency. Adding a third study on $\{2,3\}$ closes the
triangle into a cycle and creates the direct-versus-indirect tension that node-splitting
(@def-node-splitting) adjudicates. The running example of @exm-nma-running is this closed triangle with
one further multi-arm trial, and everything in this chapter is the systematic version of this enlargement.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Arm-based and contrast-based likelihoods.** The model @eq-nma-linpred is *arm-based*: the observations
are the $N$ arms. An equivalent *contrast-based* form, used for estimation and in the worked example of
@sec-nma-example, takes as data the $C$ within-study contrast estimates
$y_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}=\hat\theta_{jk}-\hat\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}$. In large samples each contrast estimate is
approximately normal about the true contrast by the delta method (@thm-delta-method), and two contrasts
that share the baseline arm of a multi-arm study are correlated because the shared arm's sampling error
enters both; @thm-re-nma-correlation computes that correlation. Passing from the arm-based to the
contrast-based likelihood is exactly the elimination of the per-study baselines $\mu_j$, which appear in
each study's arms alike and cancel in within-study differences. Concretely, in a two-arm study with
baseline arm $1$, the two arm means are $\theta_{j1}=\mu_j$ and $\theta_{j2}=\mu_j+\delta_{j,12}$;
subtracting the baseline arm removes $\mu_j$ and leaves the contrast $\delta_{j,12}=\theta_{j2}-\theta_{j1}$.
The recipe is the same in general: (i) start from the $N$ arms; (ii) in each study pick a baseline arm
$t_{j,1}$; (iii) subtract that arm's estimate from the others; (iv) keep the resulting $A_j-1$ within-study
contrasts; (v) carry their covariance, which within a multi-arm study has the shared-arm correlation of
@thm-re-nma-correlation. Steps (i) to (iv) turn $N$ arm observations into $C$ contrast observations by
discarding the $J$ baselines; step (v) is the price of that convenience. We develop both views and prove
the identifiability theory on the arm-based design, where the baselines are explicit. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Two parameterizations of the arm means {#sec-nma-param}

The arm means $\boldsymbol\theta$ carry two layers of information: the *level* of each study's outcomes,
which is a nuisance reflecting that study's population and baseline risk, and the *contrasts* between
treatments, which are the quantities of interest. The two standard parameterizations split these layers
in two different ways.

::: {#def-baseline-shift-param}
## Baseline-shift parameterization
The **baseline-shift parameterization** (corresponds to D.5 in the proof catalogue) writes each arm mean
as the study baseline plus a study-specific contrast to that baseline:
$$
\theta_{jk} \;=\; \mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}} \;+\; \delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k},
\qquad k\in\mathcal A_j,
$$ {#eq-nma-bs}
with the convention $\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}t_{j,1}}=0$ for the baseline arm, so that
$\mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}}=\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}$. The free parameters are the $J$ baselines
$\mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}}$ and the $C=N-J$ within-study contrasts
$\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}$ for the non-baseline arms $k\ne t_{j,1}$, a total of
$J+C=N$ parameters. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

In words, the baseline-shift form gives every study its own private answer: it names a separate contrast
$\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}$ inside every study. It places no
restriction on the arm means at all: there are as many parameters, $N$, as arms, and @eq-nma-bs is simply
a relabeling of the $N$ numbers $\theta_{jk}$ into $J$ baselines and $C$ within-study differences. Its
virtue is that each $\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}$ is the natural target of a random effect in the
random-effects model of @sec-nma-random. Its defect is that it does not, by itself, tie studies together:
the contrast $\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}$ of study $j$ and the contrast $\delta_{j',t_{j',1}k}$ of study $j'$
for the very same pair of treatments are, a priori, distinct parameters. Tying them together is the
content of the consistency assumption, which the second parameterization builds in from the start.

::: {#def-reference-treatment-param}
## Reference-treatment parameterization
Fix the network reference treatment $1$ and a vector of **network contrasts**
$\mathbf d=(d_2,\dots,d_K)^\top\in\mathbb R^{K-1}$, where $d_k$ is the relative effect of treatment $k$
versus the reference on the link scale, with the convention $d_1=0$. The **reference-treatment
parameterization** (corresponds to D.6 in the proof catalogue) writes
$$
\theta_{jk} \;=\; \mu_j \;+\; \bigl(d_k - d_{t_{j,1}}\bigr),
\qquad k\in\mathcal A_j,
$$ {#eq-nma-rt}
where $\mu_j=\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}$ is the study-$j$ baseline. The free parameters are the $J$ baselines
$\mu_j$ and the $K-1$ network contrasts $d_2,\dots,d_K$, a total of $J+K-1$ parameters.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

In the reference-treatment form a treatment carries a single contrast $d_k$ for the whole network. In
words, this form gives each treatment *one* number, its effect versus the reference, good for the entire
network; every study comparing two treatments must then show the same gap between them. The reference
treatment $1$ is only a coordinate origin, like the choice of where to put zero on a thermometer: it is
usually placebo for readability, but any treatment could serve, and the network's answers (any $d_{ab}$)
do not depend on the choice. The
within-study contrast of treatment $k$ versus the study baseline is forced to be
$$
\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k} \;=\; \theta_{jk}-\theta_{j,t_{j,1}} \;=\; d_k - d_{t_{j,1}} ,
$$ {#eq-nma-consistency-constraint}
the same expression in every study that compares those two treatments. Equation
@eq-nma-consistency-constraint is the **consistency constraint**: it is automatic in the
reference-treatment parameterization and is the formal statement that the relative effects are constant
across the network, the population-level constancy of @def-constancy-relative-effects rendered as an
algebraic identity among parameters. A caution on the word: *consistency* here is a property of a whole
network of relative effects (direct and indirect routes agree), and it is unrelated to the SUTVA
consistency of Chapter 9, which links an observed outcome to a potential outcome. The two ideas share only
a name. The two parameterizations therefore differ in their parameter
counts, $N$ for baseline-shift against $J+K-1$ for reference-treatment, and they agree precisely when the
within-study contrasts obey @eq-nma-consistency-constraint. Making that statement exact is the work of
@sec-nma-equivalence; first we study the algebra of the network contrasts themselves.

## Consistency equations and their algebraic closure {#sec-nma-consistency}

The reference-treatment parameterization defines a contrast only against the reference. The contrast
between any two treatments is recovered by subtraction, and the resulting family of $\binom{K}{2}$
pairwise contrasts is highly redundant. The next theorem makes the redundancy precise: the family is
generated by $K-1$ free numbers and is pinned down by a definite number of loop constraints. These
constraints are what an inconsistency analysis tests.

Before the general statement, here is the identity in the running example. Suppose the pooled effects come
out as Drug A vs placebo $d_{12}=0.5$ and Drug B vs placebo $d_{13}=1.0$ on the log-odds scale. Then
consistency forces the Drug B vs Drug A contrast to be $d_{23}=d_{13}-d_{12}=0.5$: it is not free to take
any other value. If a head-to-head trial instead reported Drug B vs Drug A as $0.1$, the gap between the
forced $0.5$ and the observed $0.1$ is exactly the disagreement that node-splitting (@sec-nma-nodesplit)
measures. The next theorem shows that this triangle identity, and its $K$-treatment generalizations, are
the *only* constraints the network imposes on its pairwise effects.

::: {#thm-consistency-closure}
## Closure of the consistency equations
Define, from a network-contrast vector $\mathbf d=(d_1,\dots,d_K)$ with $d_1=0$, the full family of
pairwise network contrasts
$$
d_{ab} \;:=\; d_b - d_a, \qquad a,b\in\{1,\dots,K\}.
$$ {#eq-nma-pairwise}
Then the following hold (corresponds to D.10 in the proof catalogue).

1. **Antisymmetry.** $d_{ab}=-d_{ba}$ for all $a,b$, and $d_{aa}=0$.

2. **Additivity (the triangle, or loop, identity).** For all $a,b,c$,
$$
d_{ab} + d_{bc} \;=\; d_{ac}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad d_{ac}-d_{bc}=d_{ab}.
$$ {#eq-nma-triangle}

3. **Generation.** Every pairwise contrast is determined by the $K-1$ basis contrasts
$d_2,\dots,d_K$ through $d_{ab}=d_{1b}-d_{1a}=d_b-d_a$.

4. **Converse and uniqueness.** Conversely, let $(e_{ab})_{a,b}$ be any family of real numbers satisfying
the additivity identity @eq-nma-triangle for all triples. Then $e$ is antisymmetric, and there is a
unique vector $\mathbf d$ with $d_1=0$ such that $e_{ab}=d_b-d_a$ for all $a,b$, namely $d_k=e_{1k}$.

5. **Count.** The set of consistent contrast families, those of the form @eq-nma-pairwise, is a linear
subspace of dimension $K-1$ inside the $\binom{K}{2}$-dimensional space of antisymmetric families.
The additivity identities therefore impose exactly
$$
\binom{K}{2}-(K-1)=\binom{K-1}{2}
$$ {#eq-nma-loopcount}
independent constraints.
:::

::: {.proof}
Parts 1 and 2 are immediate from @eq-nma-pairwise and reproduce, for the network contrasts, the
antisymmetry and additivity of relative effects proved within a single population in Chapter 14
(@lem-relative-effect-algebra). For antisymmetry, $d_{ab}=d_b-d_a=-(d_a-d_b)=-d_{ba}$, and $d_{aa}=0$.
For additivity, $d_{ab}+d_{bc}=(d_b-d_a)+(d_c-d_b)=d_c-d_a=d_{ac}$; the middle term $d_b$ cancels, and
subtracting $d_{bc}$ from both sides rearranges to $d_{ac}-d_{bc}=d_{ab}$. Part 3 is the definition
@eq-nma-pairwise read with $a$ or $b$ equal to $1$: $d_{1b}=d_b-d_1=d_b$ and
$d_{ab}=d_b-d_a=d_{1b}-d_{1a}$.

For part 4, suppose $(e_{ab})$ satisfies @eq-nma-triangle for all triples. Because the identity holds for
*every* triple, we are free to choose convenient ones. Plugging the same index into all three slots,
$a=b=c$, gives $e_{aa}+e_{aa}=e_{aa}$, so $e_{aa}=0$: the diagonal vanishes. Choosing $c=a$ gives
$e_{ab}+e_{ba}=e_{aa}=0$, so $e_{ba}=-e_{ab}$ and $e$ is antisymmetric. Define $d_k:=e_{1k}$; then $d_1=e_{11}=0$. Apply additivity to the triple $(a,1,b)$:
$e_{a1}+e_{1b}=e_{ab}$, and using antisymmetry $e_{a1}=-e_{1a}=-d_a$, so
$e_{ab}=-d_a+d_b=d_b-d_a$, as claimed. Uniqueness: if $e_{ab}=d_b-d_a=d_b'-d_a'$ for all $a,b$ with
$d_1=d_1'=0$, then taking $a=1$ gives $d_b=e_{1b}=d_b'$ for every $b$.

For part 5, let $\mathcal A\cong\mathbb R^{\binom{K}{2}}$ be the vector space of antisymmetric families,
coordinatized by the values $e_{ab}$ for $a<b$, and let $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}\subseteq\mathcal A$ be
the subset satisfying all additivity identities, the *consistent* families. The map
$T:\mathbb R^{K-1}\to\mathcal A$ sending
$(d_2,\dots,d_K)\mapsto (e_{ab})$ with $e_{ab}=d_b-d_a$ (and $d_1=0$) is linear. It is injective: if
$d_b-d_a=0$ for all $a,b$, then taking $a=1$ gives $d_b=0$ for all $b$. By parts 3 and 4 its image is
exactly $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}$. Hence $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}$ is a linear subspace with
$\dim\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}=\dim\mathbb R^{K-1}=K-1$, and its codimension in $\mathcal A$ is
$\binom{K}{2}-(K-1)$. The arithmetic
$\binom{K}{2}-(K-1)=\tfrac{K(K-1)}{2}-(K-1)=(K-1)\tfrac{K-2}{2}=\binom{K-1}{2}$
gives @eq-nma-loopcount. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and how loops carry the constraints.** In evidence-synthesis terms: of all the
pairwise relative effects in a network, only $K-1$ are genuinely free; every other is forced by the ones
already chosen, and the forcing identities are the loop equations. Those loop equations are the *only*
places inconsistency can surface, so a network can be checked for coherence exactly where it contains a
loop, and nowhere else. The count @eq-nma-loopcount has a matching graph-theoretic reading. On the
complete graph $K_K$ a spanning tree has $K-1$ edges and contains no cycle; the contrasts along the tree
edges are free and generate all others, which is part 3. Each of the remaining
$\binom{K}{2}-(K-1)=\binom{K-1}{2}$ edges closes exactly one independent cycle, and that cycle is one
additivity identity, an equation of the form
$d_{a_1a_2}+d_{a_2a_3}+\cdots+d_{a_m a_1}=0$. The number of independent constraints equals the cycle
rank of the complete graph, and a contrast is testable for inconsistency precisely when the evidence
contains an independent cycle, that is, both a direct edge and an indirect path between its endpoints.
A tree-shaped network, such as the Bucher triangle-as-path of @sec-nma-glm, has no cycle and nothing to
test. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The incidence matrix and a rank toolkit {#sec-nma-rank}

Both the equivalence of the parameterizations (@sec-nma-equivalence) and the identifiability of the
contrasts (@sec-nma-identifiability) reduce to one number: the rank of the design matrix $\mathbf X$. That
rank is in turn controlled by a single combinatorial object, the incidence matrix of the treatment graph.
This short section isolates the two linear-algebra facts we need. @lem-incidence-rank computes the rank of
a graph's incidence matrix, which will pin down the contrast columns of $\mathbf X$; @lem-nma-gram says
that a full-rank $\mathbf X$ yields an invertible weighted normal matrix, so that the generalized least
squares estimator exists and is unique. A reader in a hurry may take both lemmas on faith and skip to
@sec-nma-equivalence; the payoff they deliver is that the question "which contrasts can the network
estimate?" becomes the purely graph-theoretic "is the network connected?"

::: {#lem-incidence-rank}
## Rank of a graph incidence matrix
Let $G=(\mathcal V,\mathcal E)$ be a multigraph on $K=|\mathcal V|$ vertices, with each edge $e$ assigned
an orientation from a tail $a(e)$ to a head $b(e)$. Its **signed incidence matrix**
$\mathbf B\in\mathbb R^{|\mathcal E|\times K}$ has, in the row for edge $e$, the entry $-1$ in column
$a(e)$, the entry $+1$ in column $b(e)$, and $0$ elsewhere. If $G$ has $q$ connected components, then
$$
\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf B) \;=\; K-q .
$$ {#eq-nma-incidence-rank}
In particular $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf B)=K-1$ if and only if $G$ is connected. (We write $q$ for the
number of components to keep it distinct from the within-study contrast count $C$ of
@eq-nma-totalcontrasts.)
:::

::: {.proof}
View $\mathbf B$ as the linear map $\mathbf v\mapsto \mathbf B\mathbf v$ from $\mathbb R^K$ to
$\mathbb R^{|\mathcal E|}$. By construction the $e$-th coordinate of $\mathbf B\mathbf v$ is
$(\mathbf B\mathbf v)_e=v_{b(e)}-v_{a(e)}$. In words, $\mathbf B$ turns a labeling of the vertices, one
number $v_i$ per treatment, into the list of its differences across the edges: the row for edge $e$ reports
$v$ at the head minus $v$ at the tail. The whole proof is then the observation that the labelings which are
flat across every edge are exactly the labelings that are constant on each connected piece. Hence
$\mathbf v\in\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$ if and only if
$v_{a(e)}=v_{b(e)}$ for every edge $e$, that is, if and only if $\mathbf v$ takes equal values on the two
endpoints of every edge.

We claim $\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$ is the set of vectors that are constant on each connected component of
$G$. If $\mathbf v$ is constant on components and $e$ is an edge, its endpoints lie in the same component,
so $v_{a(e)}=v_{b(e)}$ and $\mathbf v\in\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$. Conversely, suppose $\mathbf v$ equalizes
across every edge, and let $u,w$ lie in the same component. By definition of a component there is a path
$u=x_0,x_1,\dots,x_m=w$ with each $\{x_{i-1},x_i\}\in\mathcal E$; equalizing across each edge of the path
gives $v_{x_0}=v_{x_1}=\cdots=v_{x_m}$, so $v_u=v_w$. Thus $\mathbf v$ is constant on each component.

Let $\mathcal V=\mathcal V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup\mathcal V_q$ be the partition into components and let
$\mathbf 1_{\mathcal V_i}\in\mathbb R^K$ be the indicator vector of $\mathcal V_i$. A vector is constant
on each component if and only if it is a linear combination $\sum_i \alpha_i\mathbf 1_{\mathcal V_i}$,
so these indicators span $\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$. They are linearly independent: if
$\sum_i\alpha_i\mathbf 1_{\mathcal V_i}=\mathbf 0$, then evaluating at any vertex of $\mathcal V_i$, which
is nonempty, gives $\alpha_i=0$. Hence $\dim\mathcal N(\mathbf B)=q$. By the rank-nullity theorem
(@thm-rank-nullity) applied to the map on $\mathbb R^K$,
$\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf B)=K-\dim\mathcal N(\mathbf B)=K-q$, which is @eq-nma-incidence-rank. The
final claim is the case $q=1$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What this buys us.** The incidence matrix is pure bookkeeping for which treatments are joined by
randomized comparisons. Its rank, $K$ minus the number of disconnected pieces $q$, is the number of
independent relative effects those comparisons can pin down. A connected network ($q=1$) pins down all
$K-1$ contrasts; each additional disconnected piece costs exactly one estimable contrast. This single fact
drives both theorems that follow, the equivalence of the two parameterizations and the identifiability of
the network. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#lem-nma-gram}
## Full column rank and the weighted Gram matrix
Let $\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and let $\mathbf W\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric positive
definite. Then
$$
\mathcal N(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)=\mathcal N(\mathbf X).
$$ {#eq-nma-gram-kernel}
Consequently $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$ is invertible if and only if $\mathbf X$ has full column
rank $p$, and in that case $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$ is positive definite.
:::

::: {.proof}
The inclusion $\mathcal N(\mathbf X)\subseteq\mathcal N(\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X)$ is immediate:
$\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$ gives $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$. For the reverse
inclusion, suppose $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf 0$. Then
$$
0=\mathbf v^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf v=(\mathbf X\mathbf v)^\top\mathbf W(\mathbf X\mathbf v).
$$
Since $\mathbf W$ is positive definite (@def-definiteness), $\mathbf u^\top\mathbf W\mathbf u=0$ forces
$\mathbf u=\mathbf 0$; applying this with $\mathbf u=\mathbf X\mathbf v$ gives $\mathbf X\mathbf v=\mathbf
0$, so $\mathbf v\in\mathcal N(\mathbf X)$. This proves @eq-nma-gram-kernel. The matrix
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$ is $p\times p$, hence invertible if and only if its null space is
trivial; by @eq-nma-gram-kernel this happens if and only if $\mathcal N(\mathbf X)=\{\mathbf 0\}$, that
is, if and only if $\mathbf X$ has full column rank (@lem-injective-trivial-kernel). When $\mathbf X$ has
full column rank, every $\mathbf v\ne\mathbf 0$ has $\mathbf X\mathbf v\ne\mathbf 0$ and therefore
$\mathbf v^\top\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X\mathbf v=(\mathbf X\mathbf v)^\top\mathbf W(\mathbf X\mathbf
v)>0$, so $\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$ is positive definite. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader's translation.** This is the workhorse behind every "the estimator exists and is unique" claim in
the chapter. If the columns of $\mathbf X$ are linearly independent (full column rank), then no matter what
positive-definite weighting $\mathbf W$ the data supply, the weighted normal matrix
$\mathbf X^\top\mathbf W\mathbf X$ can be inverted, so the generalized least squares formula returns one and
only one answer. Full column rank of $\mathbf X$ is thus the algebraic form of "the parameters are
estimable." $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We now assemble the reference-treatment design matrix explicitly, so that @lem-incidence-rank can be
applied to it. Order the $N$ arms arbitrarily and let $\boldsymbol\beta=(\boldsymbol\mu^\top,\mathbf
d^\top)^\top\in\mathbb R^{J+(K-1)}$ collect the baselines and the network contrasts. By @eq-nma-rt the
arm-mean vector is $\boldsymbol\theta=\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}\boldsymbol\beta$ with the block structure
$$
\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}=\bigl[\ \mathbf X_\mu \ \big|\ \mathbf X_d\ \bigr],
\qquad
\mathbf X_\mu\in\mathbb R^{N\times J},\quad \mathbf X_d\in\mathbb R^{N\times (K-1)} .
$$ {#eq-nma-design}
The baseline block $\mathbf X_\mu$ has a single $1$ in each row, in the column of the study to which that
arm belongs. The contrast block $\mathbf X_d$ has, in the row for arm $(j,k)$, a $+1$ in column $k$ and a
$-1$ in column $t_{j,1}$ (omitting any entry in the dropped column $1$, since $d_1=0$); for the baseline
arm $k=t_{j,1}$ the row of $\mathbf X_d$ is zero. Thus the rows of $\mathbf X_d$ for the $C$ non-baseline
arms are precisely the rows of the signed incidence matrix $\mathbf B$ of $G$ with column $1$ deleted,
each non-baseline arm $(j,k)$ corresponding to the oriented edge $t_{j,1}\to k$. The running example makes
this concrete: its contrast design $\mathbf X$ is written out, one row per within-study contrast, in Step
1 of @exm-nma-triangle.

## Equivalence of the two parameterizations {#sec-nma-equivalence}

We can now state in what sense the baseline-shift and reference-treatment forms describe the same model.
The baseline-shift parameterization is a *saturated* relabeling of the arm means, meaning it has exactly as
many free parameters as there are arms, so it can reproduce any pattern of arm means whatsoever and ranges
over all of $\mathbb R^N$; the reference-treatment parameterization ranges over only a subspace, the image
of the design map @eq-nma-design. The theorem identifies that subspace and shows the two forms coincide on
it.

Why prove this at all? We want to be certain that the tidy reference-treatment form, which bakes in
consistency by giving each treatment a single effect $d_k$, does not secretly discard any believable
pattern of arm means. The theorem gives that reassurance and locates the discarded directions precisely:
the reference-treatment form captures *exactly* the consistent arm-mean patterns, and the surplus
parameters that the baseline-shift form carries are precisely the directions in which real data can
disagree with consistency. That surplus is where inconsistency lives. The following table lines up the two
coordinate systems.

| Quantity | Baseline-shift name | Reference-treatment name |
|---|---|---|
| level of study $j$ | $\mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}}$ (free) | $\mu_j$ (free) |
| study-$j$ contrast of $k$ vs its baseline | $\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}$ (free) | $d_k-d_{t_{j,1}}$ (forced by @eq-nma-consistency-constraint) |
| free parameters in $\mathbb R^N$ | $N$ | $J+K-1$ |
| surplus, where inconsistency can appear | $C-(K-1)$ | $0$ |

::: {#thm-parameterization-equivalence}
## Equivalence on the consistency-constrained subspace
Consider a connected network and the reference-treatment design map
$\Phi:\mathbb R^{J}\times\mathbb R^{K-1}\to\mathbb R^{N}$,
$\Phi(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)=\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)$, of @eq-nma-design.
Define the **consistency-constrained subspace** $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}=\operatorname{image}(\Phi)
=\mathcal C(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})\subseteq\mathbb R^{N}$. Then (corresponds to D.7 in the proof
catalogue):

1. **Rank and bijection.** $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})=J+K-1$, so $\Phi$ is injective,
and $\Phi:\mathbb R^{J+K-1}\to\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$ is a linear isomorphism. In particular
$\dim\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}=J+K-1$.

2. **Characterization of the subspace.** An arm-mean vector $\boldsymbol\theta$ lies in
$\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$ if and only if its baseline-shift contrasts satisfy the consistency
constraint @eq-nma-consistency-constraint, that is, if and only if there is a vector $\mathbf d$ with
$\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}=d_k-d_{t_{j,1}}$ for every non-baseline arm $(j,k)$. On $\mathcal
S_{\mathrm{cons}}$ the correspondence between reference-treatment coordinates
$(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)$ and baseline-shift coordinates $(\boldsymbol\mu^{\mathrm{BS}},
\boldsymbol\delta)$ is a bijection.

3. **Likelihood identity.** Because the data enter the model only through the linear predictor
$\boldsymbol\theta$ (@def-glm), any two parameterizations that produce the same $\boldsymbol\theta$
produce the same likelihood. Hence on $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$ the baseline-shift and
reference-treatment models have identical likelihoods.

The two parameterizations have different free-parameter counts in $\mathbb R^N$, namely $N$ for
baseline-shift against $J+K-1$ for reference-treatment; they agree exactly on the $(J+K-1)$-dimensional
subspace $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$, where the consistency constraints remove the surplus
$N-(J+K-1)=C-(K-1)$ degrees of freedom.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Rank and injectivity (part 1).* We compute $\mathcal N(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})$. Suppose
$\Phi(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)=\mathbf 0$, that is, $\mu_j+(d_k-d_{t_{j,1}})=0$ for every arm $(j,k)$.
Apply this to the baseline arm $k=t_{j,1}$ of each study, where $d_k-d_{t_{j,1}}=0$; it gives $\mu_j=0$
for every $j$. With all baselines zero, the equation for the non-baseline arms reads
$d_k-d_{t_{j,1}}=0$ for every within-study edge $t_{j,1}\to k$, that is, $\mathbf B\tilde{\mathbf
d}=\mathbf 0$ where $\tilde{\mathbf d}=(d_1,\dots,d_K)$ is the *padded* contrast vector that restores the
dropped reference coordinate $d_1=0$ (the toolkit table of @sec-nma-running records this convention; the
unpadded $\mathbf d=(d_2,\dots,d_K)$ has length $K-1$), and $\mathbf B$ is the full signed
incidence matrix of $G$. By @lem-incidence-rank, $\tilde{\mathbf d}\in\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$ means
$\tilde{\mathbf d}$ is constant on each connected component of $G$. Since $G$ is connected,
$\tilde{\mathbf d}$ is constant on all of $\mathcal V$, and the constant equals $d_1=0$, so
$\tilde{\mathbf d}=\mathbf 0$ and hence $\mathbf d=\mathbf 0$. Thus $\mathcal N(\mathbf
X_{\mathrm{RT}})=\{\mathbf 0\}$, $\Phi$ is injective, and
$\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})=J+K-1$. An injective linear map onto its image is an
isomorphism, so $\Phi:\mathbb R^{J+K-1}\to\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$ is a linear isomorphism and
$\dim\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}=J+K-1$.

*Characterization (part 2).* The baseline-shift coordinates of any $\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathbb R^N$ are
$\mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}}=\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}$ and
$\delta_{j,\,t_{j,1}k}=\theta_{jk}-\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}$; this map
$\Psi:\boldsymbol\theta\mapsto(\boldsymbol\mu^{\mathrm{BS}},\boldsymbol\delta)$ is a linear bijection of
$\mathbb R^N$ onto $\mathbb R^J\times\mathbb R^C$, since $\boldsymbol\theta$ is recovered by
$\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}=\mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}}$ and $\theta_{jk}=\mu_j^{\mathrm{BS}}+\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}$. If
$\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$, write $\boldsymbol\theta=\Phi(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)$;
then $\theta_{jk}-\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}=(d_k-d_{t_{j,1}})-(d_{t_{j,1}}-d_{t_{j,1}})=d_k-d_{t_{j,1}}$, so the
baseline-shift contrasts satisfy @eq-nma-consistency-constraint. Conversely, if the baseline-shift
contrasts of some $\boldsymbol\theta$ satisfy $\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}=d_k-d_{t_{j,1}}$ for a vector
$\mathbf d$, set $\mu_j:=\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}$; then
$\theta_{jk}=\theta_{j,t_{j,1}}+\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}=\mu_j+(d_k-d_{t_{j,1}})=\Phi(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf
d)_{jk}$, so $\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$. The vector $\mathbf d$ is unique by the
injectivity of $\Phi$ established in part 1, so the correspondence
$(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)\leftrightarrow(\boldsymbol\mu^{\mathrm{BS}},\boldsymbol\delta)$ is a
bijection on $\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$, being the composition of the isomorphism $\Phi$ with the
bijection $\Psi$.

*Likelihood identity (part 3).* In a generalized linear model the log-likelihood is a function of the
data and of the mean vector $g^{-1}(\boldsymbol\theta)$, hence of $\boldsymbol\theta$ alone
(@def-glm); it does not see the parameterization that produced $\boldsymbol\theta$. If
$(\boldsymbol\mu^{\mathrm{BS}},\boldsymbol\delta)$ and $(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)$ are matched
coordinates of the same $\boldsymbol\theta\in\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}$, as in part 2, they yield the
same $\boldsymbol\theta$ and therefore the same likelihood value. The dimension bookkeeping is the
difference of the two parameter counts established in @def-baseline-shift-param and
@def-reference-treatment-param, $N-(J+K-1)=(N-J)-(K-1)=C-(K-1)$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why the surplus is harmless and where it bites.** A naming caution first: the arm-mean subspace
$\mathcal S_{\mathrm{cons}}\subseteq\mathbb R^N$ used here and the contrast-family space
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{cons}}$ of @thm-consistency-closure both encode consistency, but they live in
different spaces, one of arm means and one of pairwise contrasts; do not conflate them. When the network
has only two-arm studies and no
repeated comparisons, $C=K-1$ and the two parameterizations have the same count; baseline-shift and
reference-treatment are then merely two coordinate systems on the same space. The surplus $C-(K-1)$ is
strictly positive exactly when some treatments are compared more than once, either by a multi-arm study,
which contributes $A_j-1>1$ contrasts, or by several studies sharing a treatment pair. In those cases the
baseline-shift form has genuinely more names than parameters, and the consistency constraints
@eq-nma-consistency-constraint, automatic under reference-treatment, become substantive equalities that
the data can contradict. That possibility of contradiction is inconsistency, and @sec-nma-nodesplit makes
it testable. The reference-treatment parameterization is, in this sense, the minimal description of a
consistent network. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Fixed-effect identifiability {#sec-nma-identifiability}

In the fixed-effect model the within-study contrasts obey the consistency constraint exactly, so the
parameters are $(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)$ and the model is the reference-treatment generalized linear
model with design @eq-nma-design. Identifiability of the network contrasts is then a clean rank
condition, and the rank is settled by @lem-incidence-rank. The headline is blunt and worth stating before
the proof: if the network is disconnected, no statistical method can estimate a contrast between the
disconnected pieces; identifiability *is* connectivity, full stop. Everything below makes that precise and
says what to do instead.

::: {#thm-fe-nma-identifiability}
## Fixed-effect NMA is identifiable iff the network is connected
Consider the fixed-effect network model $\boldsymbol\theta=\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}\boldsymbol\beta$ with
$\boldsymbol\beta=(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)$, and a working covariance $\mathbf V\succ 0$ for the
arm-level (or contrast-level) data. Let $q$ be the number of connected components of the
treatment-comparison graph $G$ (the same $q$ as in @lem-incidence-rank, kept distinct from the contrast
count $C$). Then (corresponds to D.8 in the proof catalogue):

1. $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})=J+K-q$. In particular the design has full column rank
$J+K-1$ if and only if $G$ is connected.

2. The following are equivalent: (a) $G$ is connected; (b) $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}$ has full column
rank; (c) the weighted normal matrix $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}$
is invertible; (d) the parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$ is identifiable, meaning distinct $\boldsymbol\beta$
give distinct mean vectors; (e) the generalized least squares estimator
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\bigl(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}\bigr)^{-1}
\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf y
$$ {#eq-nma-gls}
exists and is the unique minimizer of the weighted least squares objective
$(\mathbf y-\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}\boldsymbol\beta)^\top\mathbf V^{-1}(\mathbf y-\mathbf
X_{\mathrm{RT}}\boldsymbol\beta)$, and is then the best linear unbiased estimator of $\boldsymbol\beta$.

3. When $G$ is disconnected, every contrast $d_{ab}$ between treatments in different components is
non-identifiable: it can be changed without changing the distribution of the data.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Part 1.* From the kernel computation in the proof of @thm-parameterization-equivalence, any
$(\boldsymbol\mu,\mathbf d)\in\mathcal N(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})$ has $\boldsymbol\mu=\mathbf 0$ forced
by the baseline-arm rows, and $\tilde{\mathbf d}=(0,d_2,\dots,d_K)$ lying in $\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$. By
@lem-incidence-rank, $\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$ is the span of the $q$ component indicators and has
dimension $q$; intersecting with the hyperplane $\{d_1=0\}$ removes exactly one dimension, the one along
the indicator of the component containing vertex $1$, leaving a space of dimension $q-1$. Hence
$\dim\mathcal N(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})=q-1$, and by rank-nullity
$\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})=(J+K-1)-(q-1)=J+K-q$. For $q=1$ this is the full column
rank $J+K-1$; for $q>1$ it is strictly smaller.

*Part 2.* (a)$\Leftrightarrow$(b) is the $q=1$ case of part 1. (b)$\Leftrightarrow$(c) is
@lem-nma-gram with $\mathbf W=\mathbf V^{-1}\succ 0$. For (b)$\Rightarrow$(d): if $\mathbf
X_{\mathrm{RT}}$ has full column rank then $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto\boldsymbol\theta=\mathbf
X_{\mathrm{RT}}\boldsymbol\beta$ is injective, and since the mean vector $g^{-1}(\boldsymbol\theta)$ is a
coordinatewise strictly monotone, hence injective, function of $\boldsymbol\theta$, distinct
$\boldsymbol\beta$ give distinct means and so distinct distributions; this is identifiability. For
(d)$\Rightarrow$(b): contrapositively, if $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}$ is column-rank-deficient there is
$\boldsymbol\beta_0\ne\mathbf 0$ with $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}\boldsymbol\beta_0=\mathbf 0$, so
$\boldsymbol\beta$ and $\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\beta_0$ give the same $\boldsymbol\theta$ and the
same distribution, contradicting identifiability. For (c)$\Rightarrow$(e): invertibility of
$\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}^\top\mathbf V^{-1}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}$ makes @eq-nma-gls well defined.
Writing $\mathbf V^{-1/2}$ for the symmetric positive definite square root of $\mathbf V^{-1}$
(@prp-matrix-square-root) and whitening, $\tilde{\mathbf y}=\mathbf V^{-1/2}\mathbf y$,
$\tilde{\mathbf X}=\mathbf V^{-1/2}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}$, the weighted objective becomes the ordinary
sum of squares $\|\tilde{\mathbf y}-\tilde{\mathbf X}\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2$, whose unique minimizer is
the ordinary least squares estimator
$(\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf X})^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top\tilde{\mathbf y}=\hat{\boldsymbol
\beta}$ of @eq-nma-gls, unique because $\tilde{\mathbf X}=\mathbf V^{-1/2}\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}$ has the
same trivial kernel as $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}$. The whitened errors have covariance
$\mathbf V^{-1/2}\mathbf V\mathbf V^{-1/2}=I$, so the Gauss-Markov theorem (@thm-ols-blue) applies to the
whitened model and makes $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ the best linear unbiased estimator. Finally
(e)$\Rightarrow$(c) holds because @eq-nma-gls requires the inverse to exist. This closes the cycle of
equivalences.

*Part 3.* Suppose $a$ and $b$ lie in different components $\mathcal V_i\ne\mathcal V_{i'}$ of $G$.
Construct $\boldsymbol\beta_0=(\mathbf 0,\mathbf d_0)$ with $\tilde{\mathbf d}_0=\mathbf 1_{\mathcal
V_{i'}}$ if $1\notin\mathcal V_{i'}$, or $\tilde{\mathbf d}_0=\mathbf 1_{\mathcal V_i}$ if instead
$1\notin\mathcal V_i$ (at least one of the two components omits vertex $1$). Then $\tilde{\mathbf
d}_0\in\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$ with $d_{0,1}=0$, so $\boldsymbol\beta_0\in\mathcal N(\mathbf
X_{\mathrm{RT}})$ by part 1, and $\boldsymbol\beta_0$ changes $d_{ab}=d_b-d_a$ by
$\pm 1\ne 0$ while leaving $\boldsymbol\theta$, hence the distribution, unchanged. Thus $d_{ab}$ is
non-identifiable. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Plain-language takeaway.** In practice: if every treatment can be reached from every other by following
trial comparisons, the fixed-effect NMA can estimate all relative effects, direct or indirect. If it
cannot, the missing cross-cluster contrasts are lost to statistics entirely; no amount of clever pooling
recovers them. The only remedies are to find a trial that bridges the gap, or to bring in an external
assumption that supplies the missing link, which is the business of the population-adjustment methods of
Part V. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The estimable contrasts of a disconnected network.** For a concrete picture, suppose trials of Drug A
versus placebo and Drug B versus placebo form one cluster $\{\text{placebo},\text{A},\text{B}\}$, while a
separate group of trials compares Drug C against Drug D, with no trial ever linking the two groups:

```
   placebo --- Drug A          Drug C --- Drug D
      |
   Drug B
```

Here $q=2$ components. Within the first cluster, Drug A versus Drug B is identifiable (the two are
connected through placebo); but Drug A versus Drug C is not, because one may add any constant to *both*
Drug C's and Drug D's effects without changing a single observed within-study contrast. Part 3 shows that
cross-component contrasts vanish
from the identifiable parameters, but within each connected component the analysis goes through verbatim:
restricting to a component with $K_i$ treatments and its studies gives a connected subnetwork whose
$K_i-1$ contrasts are identifiable. A disconnected network is therefore not useless; it is several
separate networks, and no indirect comparison can bridge them without an external assumption. Bridging
disconnected components is exactly the task that unanchored population adjustment confronts in Part V,
where the missing edge is supplied by modeling absolute outcomes rather than contrasts. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Random-effects NMA and the one-half correlation {#sec-nma-random}

The single most actionable warning in this chapter lives in this section: a three-arm trial is not two
independent two-arm trials. Its within-trial contrasts share an arm, so their sampling errors are
correlated; treating them as independent, a genuinely common mistake in practice, produces wrong standard
errors. Below we derive that correlation and show it is not an arbitrary modeling choice but a forced
value.

One caution before we start. Random effects model *heterogeneity*, the scatter of study-level effects
around shared network effects; they do not repair *inconsistency*, the disagreement of direct and indirect
routes. A random-effects NMA still assumes the network is consistent in expectation. Heterogeneity is
variation around the network effects; inconsistency is a conflict between them, and no heterogeneity
variance can absorb it.

Fixed-effect NMA assumes the within-study contrasts equal the network contrasts exactly. The
random-effects model (@def-random-effects) relaxes this: the study-level contrasts vary about the network
contrasts with a heterogeneity variance $\tau^2$, just as in pairwise random-effects meta-analysis
(@thm-dersimonian-laird, @def-i-squared). In a multi-arm study the several contrasts to the shared
baseline are then correlated, and the correlation takes a universal value. We first show that the value
is forced by a symmetry requirement, then exhibit the construction that realizes it.

::: {#lem-half-correlation-forced}
## The one-half correlation is forced by basis invariance
Let a study compare arms $1,2,\dots,m+1$ with arm $1$ the baseline, and let the random within-study
contrasts $\delta_{1k}:=\delta_{j,1k}$ ($k=2,\dots,m+1$) have an exchangeable covariance: equal variances
$\operatorname{Var}(\delta_{1k})=v$ and equal pairwise covariances
$\operatorname{Cov}(\delta_{1k},\delta_{1l})=\rho v$ for $k\ne l$. Suppose the heterogeneity variance is
required to be the same for every contrast in the study regardless of which arm is named the baseline,
that is, $\operatorname{Var}(\delta_{1l}-\delta_{1k})=v$ for the derived contrast $\delta_{kl}$ of arm
$l$ versus arm $k$. Then necessarily
$$
\rho=\tfrac12 .
$$ {#eq-nma-half}
:::

::: {.proof}
The derived contrast of arm $l$ versus arm $k$ is $\delta_{kl}=\delta_{1l}-\delta_{1k}$, since
$(\theta_l-\theta_1)-(\theta_k-\theta_1)=\theta_l-\theta_k$. Its variance is
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\delta_{1l}-\delta_{1k})
=\operatorname{Var}(\delta_{1l})+\operatorname{Var}(\delta_{1k})-2\operatorname{Cov}(\delta_{1l},\delta_{1k})
=v+v-2\rho v=2v(1-\rho).
$$
Setting this equal to $v$, the common heterogeneity variance, and dividing by $v>0$ gives $2(1-\rho)=1$,
hence $\rho=\tfrac12$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader's translation.** The lemma answers the question "why exactly one half, and not some other
correlation?" The answer is a symmetry demand: the heterogeneity of a treatment comparison should not
change if we rename which arm is called the baseline. Only the correlation $1/2$ makes every derived
contrast carry the same variance $v$ as the originals; any other value would make the measured
heterogeneity depend on an arbitrary bookkeeping choice. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The requirement in @lem-half-correlation-forced is natural: the heterogeneity of a treatment effect
across studies should not depend on the bookkeeping choice of which treatment is written as the
reference. The unique covariance compatible with that invariance is the one with all correlations equal
to one half. The following construction shows that this covariance arises from the simplest possible
generative assumption, exchangeable arm-level random effects, and computes it for any number of arms. One
notational point to flag before the statement: the construction writes the arm-level variance as
$\tau^2/2$, not $\tau^2$, and this is deliberate. Each contrast is a difference of two independent arm
effects, so its variance is $\tau^2/2+\tau^2/2=\tau^2$; the half on the arms is chosen precisely so that
the *contrast* variance comes out to the network heterogeneity $\tau^2$. Read $\tau^2/2$ as "whatever
arm-level variance makes the contrasts have variance $\tau^2$."

::: {#thm-re-nma-correlation}
## Contrast correlation in a multi-arm trial is one half
Model each treatment's true effect in study $j$ as $\eta_{jk}=d_k+u_{jk}$, where $d_1=0$, the network
contrast of treatment $k$ is $d_k$, and the arm-level random effects $u_{jk}$ are independent across
treatments and studies with $u_{jk}\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2/2)$. Then the within-study contrasts to the
baseline arm $1$, namely $\delta_{j,1k}=\eta_{jk}-\eta_{j1}$ for $k=2,\dots,A_j$, satisfy (corresponds to
D.9 in the proof catalogue)
$$
\mathbb E[\delta_{j,1k}]=d_k,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\delta_{j,1k})=\tau^2,\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\delta_{j,1k},\delta_{j,1l})=\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}\ (k\ne l),
$$ {#eq-nma-re-moments}
so the correlation between any two contrasts sharing the baseline arm is $\tfrac12$. Stacking the
$(A_j-1)$ contrasts, their covariance matrix is
$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma_j
=\tau^2\,\frac{I_{A_j-1}+J_{A_j-1}}{2},
$$ {#eq-nma-re-cov}
where $J_m=\mathbf 1_m\mathbf 1_m^\top$ is the $m\times m$ all-ones matrix (every entry equal to $1$).
This matrix is positive definite, with eigenvalues
$\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}(A_j)$ once and $\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}$ with multiplicity $A_j-2$, and determinant
$\det\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=A_j\,(\tau^2/2)^{A_j-1}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Since $d_1=0$ and $u_{j1}\sim\mathcal N(0,\tau^2/2)$, the contrast is
$\delta_{j,1k}=\eta_{jk}-\eta_{j1}=(d_k+u_{jk})-u_{j1}$, whose mean is $d_k$. Using independence of the
arm-level effects,
$$
\operatorname{Var}(\delta_{j,1k})=\operatorname{Var}(u_{jk})+\operatorname{Var}(u_{j1})
=\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}+\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}=\tau^2 .
$$
For $k\ne l$, both different from $1$, bilinearity of covariance and the independence of distinct
arm-level effects give
$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\delta_{j,1k},\delta_{j,1l})
=\operatorname{Cov}(u_{jk}-u_{j1},\,u_{jl}-u_{j1})
=\operatorname{Cov}(u_{jk},u_{jl})-\operatorname{Cov}(u_{jk},u_{j1})-\operatorname{Cov}(u_{j1},u_{jl})
+\operatorname{Var}(u_{j1}),
$$
in which the first three terms vanish and the last equals $\tau^2/2$. The correlation is
$(\tau^2/2)/\tau^2=\tfrac12$, which is @eq-nma-re-moments. Writing $m=A_j-1$, the covariance matrix has
diagonal entries $\tau^2$ and off-diagonal entries $\tau^2/2$, that is,
$\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}(I_m+J_m)$, the matrix @eq-nma-re-cov.

For the spectrum, $J_m=\mathbf 1_m\mathbf 1_m^\top$ has eigenvalue $m$ with eigenvector
$\mathbf 1_m$ (since $J_m\mathbf 1_m=m\mathbf 1_m$) and eigenvalue $0$ with multiplicity $m-1$ on the
orthogonal complement $\{\mathbf v:\mathbf 1_m^\top\mathbf v=0\}$. Hence $I_m+J_m$ has eigenvalue
$1+m=A_j$ once and $1$ with multiplicity $m-1=A_j-2$, and $\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}(I_m+J_m)$
has eigenvalues $\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}A_j$ and $\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}$ as stated (@thm-spectral-theorem). All
eigenvalues are positive for $\tau^2>0$, so $\boldsymbol\Sigma_j\succ 0$ (@thm-pd-characterization); the
determinant is the product of the eigenvalues,
$\det\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}A_j\cdot(\tfrac{\tau^2}{2})^{A_j-2}=A_j(\tau^2/2)^{A_j-1}$.
$\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The same one-half in the sampling covariance.** The one-half of @thm-re-nma-correlation governs the
*heterogeneity* covariance of the random contrasts. An identical one-half appears in the *sampling*
covariance of the contrast estimates from a multi-arm trial when the arms have equal precision: if
$\hat\eta_{jk}$ are independent arm estimates with common variance $\sigma^2$, then the shared baseline
arm makes
$\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\eta_{jk}-\hat\eta_{j1},\hat\eta_{jl}-\hat\eta_{j1})=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\eta_{j1})=\sigma^2$,
while each contrast has variance $2\sigma^2$, so the correlation is again $\tfrac12$. This is the
positive covariance flagged after @thm-bucher-variance, the reason a single three-arm trial cannot be
treated as two independent two-arm trials. The worked example of @sec-nma-example uses equal-precision
arms, so its multi-arm sampling block has correlation exactly one half. Numerically, its study $4$ gives
two contrasts each with variance $0.20$ and covariance $0.10$, correlation exactly $1/2$; their difference
(the derived Drug A versus Drug B contrast) has variance $0.20+0.20-2(0.10)=0.20$, the same as each
original contrast, which is the invariance @lem-half-correlation-forced demanded. Treating the two study-4
contrasts as independent would instead give $0.20+0.20=0.40$, doubling the apparent variance and
misstating the precision of every multi-arm comparison. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Inconsistency and node-splitting {#sec-nma-nodesplit}

When a contrast is informed by both a direct comparison and one or more indirect paths, the consistency
equations of @thm-consistency-closure become falsifiable. Node-splitting compares the two streams of
evidence at a chosen contrast and tests whether they agree. We first record the fact that lets us speak
of a single indirect estimate: the network pools a contrast's direct and indirect evidence by
inverse-variance weighting.

::: {#prp-network-contrast-pooling}
## A contrast is the inverse-variance blend of its direct and indirect evidence
Suppose a contrast $d_{AB}$ is informed by two independent sources, a direct estimate
$\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}$ with variance $v_{\mathrm{dir}}$ and an indirect estimate
$\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB}$ with variance $v_{\mathrm{ind}}$, both unbiased for $d_{AB}$. The
fixed-effect network estimate combining the two sources is the inverse-variance-weighted mean
$$
\hat d^{\mathrm{net}}_{AB}
=\frac{w_{\mathrm{dir}}\,\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}+w_{\mathrm{ind}}\,\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB}}
{w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}}},
\qquad
w_{\mathrm{dir}}=\frac1{v_{\mathrm{dir}}},\quad w_{\mathrm{ind}}=\frac1{v_{\mathrm{ind}}},
$$ {#eq-nma-pooling}
with variance $1/(w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}})$, and this is the best linear unbiased estimate of
$d_{AB}$ from the two sources.
:::

::: {.proof}
The two sources are independent unbiased estimators of the same scalar $d_{AB}$, so this is exactly the
two-study fixed-effect meta-analysis of Chapter 13: the inverse-variance-weighted mean @eq-nma-pooling is
the best linear unbiased combination, with the stated variance, by @thm-fixed-effect-blue (the
$k=2$ case). Independence makes the variance of @eq-nma-pooling equal to
$(w_{\mathrm{dir}}^2v_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}}^2v_{\mathrm{ind}})/(w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}})^2
=(w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}})/(w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}})^2=1/(w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}})$.
$\square$
:::

::: {#def-node-splitting}
## Node-splitting
Let $d_{AB}$ be a contrast for which the network contains both direct evidence (one or more studies
comparing $A$ and $B$) and indirect evidence (a path through other treatments). **Node-splitting**
separates the evidence on this contrast into the direct estimate $\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}$, computed
from the $AB$ studies alone, and the indirect estimate $\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB}$, computed from the
network with the direct $AB$ evidence removed. The **inconsistency statistic** for the contrast is their
difference,
$$
\hat\omega_{AB}:=\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}-\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB}
$$ {#eq-nma-omega}
(corresponds to D.11 in the proof catalogue). A node-split model is the network model in which the single
consistency equation for $d_{AB}$ is released, letting the direct and indirect contrasts differ by
$\omega_{AB}$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader's translation, and the name.** "Node-splitting" is a slightly misleading name: the method splits
the *evidence for a comparison*, a contrast such as $d_{AB}$, into its direct and indirect streams; it does
not split a single treatment node. Operationally the indirect estimate is computed by refitting the whole
network by generalized least squares with the direct $AB$ rows deleted, then reading off the $AB$ contrast;
@exm-nma-triangle, Step 5, carries this out on the running example. The statistic $\hat\omega_{AB}$ is
attached to the edge $AB$, one node-split per contrast that carries both kinds of evidence.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-node-split-test}
## Distribution of the inconsistency statistic
Assume the direct and indirect evidence streams are independent, $\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}$ is unbiased
for $d_{AB}$ with variance $\operatorname{Var}(\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB})$, and the indirect estimate is
formed along the path $A\to C\to B$ by the Bucher rule $\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat
d_{BC}$ of @thm-bucher-unbiased. Under the null hypothesis $H_0$ that the consistency equation
@eq-nma-triangle holds for the triangle $\{A,B,C\}$,
$$
\mathbb E[\hat\omega_{AB}]=0,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\omega_{AB})
=\operatorname{Var}(\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB})+\operatorname{Var}(\hat d_{AC})+\operatorname{Var}(\hat
d_{BC}),
$$ {#eq-nma-omega-moments}
and the standardized statistic $\hat\omega_{AB}/\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\omega_{AB})$ is
approximately standard normal in large samples.
:::

::: {.proof}
The direct estimate is unbiased by hypothesis, $\mathbb E[\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB}]=d_{AB}$. The
indirect estimate is the Bucher estimator, unbiased for $d_{AC}-d_{BC}$ by @thm-bucher-unbiased; under
$H_0$ the consistency equation @eq-nma-triangle gives $d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}$, so $\mathbb E[\hat
d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB}]=d_{AB}$ as well. Subtracting, $\mathbb E[\hat\omega_{AB}]=d_{AB}-d_{AB}=0$. For the
variance, the direct stream is independent of the two indirect studies, and within the indirect estimate
the studies $AC$ and $BC$ are independent, so by the variance-of-a-difference identity (@thm-bucher-variance)
$\operatorname{Var}(\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB})=\operatorname{Var}(\hat d_{AC})+\operatorname{Var}(\hat
d_{BC})$, and adding the independent direct variance gives @eq-nma-omega-moments. The asymptotic
normality of $\hat\omega_{AB}$ follows from that of its three independent, asymptotically normal
constituents (@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality, @thm-delta-method), and standardizing by a consistent
standard-error estimate yields the standard normal reference. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading a node-split, and its limits.** A small $|\hat\omega_{AB}|$ relative to its standard error is
the empirical signature of consistency on that loop; a large value signals that direct and indirect
evidence disagree, which under the structural account of Chapter 14 (@sec-bucher-failure) points to an
effect modifier (@def-effect-modifier) distributed differently across the studies in the loop, breaking
transitivity (@def-transitivity). Two cautions attend the test. First, it has the variance
@eq-nma-omega-moments, a sum of three variances, so it is often underpowered; a non-significant node-split
is weak evidence of consistency, not proof of it. Second, by @prp-network-contrast-pooling the full
network estimate of $d_{AB}$ is the inverse-variance blend @eq-nma-pooling of the very direct and
indirect estimates the node-split compares, so a strong inconsistency means the pooled estimate
averages two genuinely discordant numbers and should not be trusted without explanation. A global check
compares, by the deviance information criterion of @def-dic, the consistency model against an
inconsistency model that frees all loops, the unrelated-mean-effects model; a large drop in fit on
freeing the loops is network-level inconsistency. The detailed bias calculation behind a transitivity
failure, and its interaction with non-collapsibility (@def-non-collapsibility) and ecological bias
(@def-ecological-bias), is the subject of Chapter 16 (@thm-failure-of-bucher). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Individual-patient-data network meta-regression {#sec-nma-ipd}

This section is a bridge to Parts IV and V, not part of the core standard-NMA toolkit; a reader meeting
NMA for the first time can note the result and return to it later. Its importance is that it is the point
where patient covariates, and therefore effect modifiers, formally enter the model, which is exactly what
the population-adjustment methods will exploit.

When individual patient data (IPD) are available, the covariates of each patient can enter the linear
predictor, and treatment-by-covariate interactions, the effect modifiers, can be estimated rather than
assumed away. The resulting model is the bridge from standard NMA to the population-adjustment methods of
Parts IV and V. Concretely, imagine one covariate, baseline LDL cholesterol. Then the prognostic main
effect $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ measures how LDL shifts every patient's outcome regardless of treatment, while
the interaction $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ measures how Drug $k$'s benefit itself changes with LDL, that is,
LDL acting as an effect modifier. Condition (iii) below, within-study covariate variation, is the demand
that LDL vary among patients inside each trial, not only between trials, so that these slopes can be read
off within a study.

::: {#thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability}
## The IPD network meta-regression and its identifiability
For individual $i$ in study $j$ on arm $k$, with covariate vector $\mathbf x_{ijk}\in\mathbb R^{p}$, the
**IPD network meta-regression** (corresponds to D.12 in the proof catalogue) models the link-scale mean
as
$$
g\bigl(\mathbb E[Y_{ijk}]\bigr)
=\mu_j+\mathbf x_{ijk}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1+d_k+\mathbf x_{ijk}^\top\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k},
$$ {#eq-nma-ipdnmr}
with study baselines $\mu_j$, prognostic main effects $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ (@def-prognostic-variable),
network treatment contrasts $d_k$ ($d_1=0$), and treatment-by-covariate interactions
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ (@def-effect-modifier; $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,1}=\mathbf 0$). Assume

(i) **shared interactions:** $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ depends on the treatment $k$ and not on the study,
so it is one vector per treatment across the network;

(ii) **connectedness:** the treatment-comparison graph $G$ is connected;

(iii) **within-study covariate variation:** for each study $j$ the within-study covariate covariance
matrix is nonsingular, so the covariates are not collinear and not constant within a study;

(iv) **multi-arm anchoring:** each study has at least two arms.

Then the parameters $(\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\beta_1,\mathbf d,\{\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\}_{k\ge2})$
are identifiable: distinct parameter vectors give distinct conditional-mean functions on the observed
arms and covariate supports.
:::

::: {.proof}
Identifiability means the map from parameters to the collection of conditional-mean functions is
injective. Suppose two parameter vectors, unprimed and primed, induce the same conditional mean on every
observed arm $(j,k)$ and at every covariate value $\mathbf x$ in that arm's support. Equating
@eq-nma-ipdnmr for the two vectors, for each present arm $(j,k)$ and all $\mathbf x$ in its support,
$$
\bigl(\mu_j+d_k\bigr)+\mathbf x^\top\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}\bigr)
=\bigl(\mu_j'+d_k'\bigr)+\mathbf x^\top\bigl(\boldsymbol\beta_1'+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}'\bigr).
$$ {#eq-nma-ipd-match}
By (iii) the covariate support within study $j$ affinely spans $\mathbb R^{p}$, and randomization gives
each arm of study $j$ that same support; an affine function $\mathbf x\mapsto a+\mathbf x^\top\mathbf b$
that is identically equal to another on an affinely spanning set must agree in both its constant and its
linear part. Matching @eq-nma-ipd-match therefore yields, for each present arm $(j,k)$, the slope
identity and the intercept identity
$$
\boldsymbol\beta_1+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\boldsymbol\beta_1'+\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}',
\qquad
\mu_j+d_k=\mu_j'+d_k'.
$$ {#eq-nma-ipd-sep}

*Contrasts.* Fix a study $j$ and two of its arms $k,k'$, which exist by (iv). Differencing the intercept
identity across the two arms cancels $\mu_j$ and $\mu_j'$:
$d_k-d_{k'}=d_k'-d_{k'}'$. As $(k,k')$ ranges over the edges of $G$ this says
$\mathbf B\,\tilde{\mathbf d}=\mathbf B\,\tilde{\mathbf d}'$, where $\tilde{\mathbf
d}=(d_1,\dots,d_K)$, so $\tilde{\mathbf d}-\tilde{\mathbf d}'\in\mathcal N(\mathbf B)$. By (ii) and
@lem-incidence-rank, $\tilde{\mathbf d}-\tilde{\mathbf d}'$ is constant on the single component; since
$d_1=d_1'=0$ the constant is $0$, so $\mathbf d=\mathbf d'$.

*Interactions.* Differencing the slope identity @eq-nma-ipd-sep across the same two arms $k,k'$ of study
$j$ cancels $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ and $\boldsymbol\beta_1'$:
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k'}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}'-\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k'}'$. By (i)
each $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$ is a single network-level vector, so this holds along every edge of $G$;
applying @lem-incidence-rank coordinatewise (to each of the $p$ components of the interaction vectors),
connectedness (ii) and the normalization $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,1}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,1}'=\mathbf 0$ force
$\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}=\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}'$ for every $k$.

*Main effects and baselines.* With the interactions equal, the slope identity @eq-nma-ipd-sep for any
present arm gives $\boldsymbol\beta_1=\boldsymbol\beta_1'$. With the contrasts equal, the intercept
identity gives $\mu_j=\mu_j'$ for every study. All parameters coincide, so the parameter map is
injective. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What each hypothesis buys, and the failure modes.** The proof spends connectedness (ii) twice, once to
propagate the treatment contrasts and once to propagate the interaction contrasts along the same graph;
it spends within-study variation (iii) to read slopes off each arm, and the shared-interaction
assumption (i) to make the interaction a single vector per treatment that connectedness can propagate.
Removing any one breaks identifiability in a definite way. A disconnected network leaves cross-component
contrasts and interaction contrasts unidentified, as in @thm-fe-nma-identifiability. If a covariate is
constant within every study, varying only between studies, then within-study differencing cannot separate
$\mathbf x^\top\boldsymbol\beta_1$ from the baseline $\mu_j$, and $\boldsymbol\beta_1$ is identified only
from study-level aggregates, confounded with the baseline; this is the seed of ecological bias
(@def-ecological-bias). A treatment that appears in only one study with degenerate covariate variation
has an unidentified interaction $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}$. And if the interactions are *not* shared, each
study carrying its own $\boldsymbol\beta_{2,k}^{(j)}$, the parameter count grows by a factor of order $J$
and small networks cannot support estimation; the shared-effect-modifier assumption is then a necessity,
not a convenience, and is the load-bearing assumption of the multilevel network meta-regression of
Part V. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Residual deviance and the deviance information criterion {#sec-nma-deviance}

This section is a practical checklist rather than new network theory. The residual deviance is the
goodness-of-fit deviance of the generalized linear model of Chapter 7, and the deviance information
criterion is the Bayesian model-comparison tool of Chapter 8, each specialized to a network; a reader
focused on identifiability can skim it and return when fitting a real model.

A fitted network model must be checked, and competing models, fixed against random effects, consistency
against inconsistency, must be compared. Two summaries do this work in the applied literature: the
residual deviance, which measures absolute fit against a saturated model, and the deviance information
criterion, which trades fit against effective complexity. Both specialize the general deviance of Chapter
7 (@def-deviance, @def-saturated-model) to the network setting.

::: {#def-residual-deviance}
## Residual deviance
For an arm with data $y$ and fitted mean $\hat\mu$ under a one-parameter exponential-family likelihood,
the **deviance residual contribution** is twice the log-likelihood ratio between the saturated model,
which fits the datum exactly, and the fitted model (@def-deviance). For a binomial arm
$y_{jk}\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n_{jk},p_{jk})$ with fitted success probability $\hat p_{jk}$ (corresponds to
D.13 in the proof catalogue),
$$
D_{jk}=2\left[\,y_{jk}\log\!\frac{y_{jk}}{n_{jk}\hat p_{jk}}
+(n_{jk}-y_{jk})\log\!\frac{n_{jk}-y_{jk}}{n_{jk}(1-\hat p_{jk})}\,\right],
$$ {#eq-nma-deviance-binom}
with the convention $0\log 0=0$. The **residual deviance** of the network is the sum
$D_{\mathrm{res}}=\sum_{j,k}D_{jk}$ over all arms. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Derivation of @eq-nma-deviance-binom.** The binomial log-likelihood, dropping the constant binomial
coefficient, is $\ell(p;y)=y\log p+(n-y)\log(1-p)$. The saturated model maximizes $\ell$ over $p$ freely;
setting the derivative $y/p-(n-y)/(1-p)$ to zero gives $\hat p^{\mathrm{sat}}=y/n$. The deviance
