contribution is twice the gap between saturated and fitted log-likelihoods,
$$
D_{jk}=2\bigl[\ell(y_{jk}/n_{jk};y_{jk})-\ell(\hat p_{jk};y_{jk})\bigr]
=2\Bigl[y_{jk}\log\tfrac{y_{jk}/n_{jk}}{\hat p_{jk}}
+(n_{jk}-y_{jk})\log\tfrac{(n_{jk}-y_{jk})/n_{jk}}{1-\hat p_{jk}}\Bigr],
$$
which rearranges to @eq-nma-deviance-binom. Each term is nonnegative because the saturated model maximizes
the likelihood (@prp-deviance-nonneg). Under a correctly specified model with $N$ arms and $p$ estimated
parameters, $D_{\mathrm{res}}$ is approximately $\chi^2_{N-p}$ (@thm-deviance-test), so the posterior mean
of $D_{\mathrm{res}}$ should be close to the residual degrees of freedom $N-p$; a value far in excess
signals lack of fit, often inconsistency or unmodeled heterogeneity. As a working rule of thumb from the
applied network guidance of @dias2018nma, a well-fitting model has $D_{\mathrm{res}}$ near $N-p$ (each data
point contributes about $1$, since a $\chi^2_{N-p}$ variable has mean $N-p$), whereas a $D_{\mathrm{res}}$
several times larger than $N-p$ is a warning; the yardstick is always the residual degrees of freedom
$N-p$, not any fixed number. For a normal likelihood with known
variances the deviance contribution reduces to the squared standardized residual, and the residual
deviance is the weighted residual sum of squares, as the worked example illustrates. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-dic}
## Deviance information criterion
Let $\boldsymbol\xi$ be the model parameters with posterior $\pi(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)$, and let
$D(\boldsymbol\xi)=-2\log p(\mathbf y\mid\boldsymbol\xi)$ be the deviance. Define the posterior mean
deviance and the effective number of parameters
$$
\bar D=\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y}[D(\boldsymbol\xi)],
\qquad
p_D=\bar D-D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}),
\qquad \bar{\boldsymbol\xi}=\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y].
$$ {#eq-nma-dic-parts}
The **deviance information criterion** (corresponds to D.14 in the proof catalogue) is
$$
\mathrm{DIC}=\bar D+p_D=2\bar D-D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}).
$$ {#eq-nma-dic}
Smaller DIC indicates better posterior fit penalized for effective complexity. The conventional reading,
that DIC differences below about $3$ are not meaningful while differences above $5$ are substantial, is a
rule of thumb from the network meta-analysis guidance of @dias2018nma, not a theorem; it is a rough
calibration against the Monte Carlo and modeling noise in a DIC, and it is no substitute for clinical
judgment about whether transitivity holds. In applied use DIC most often compares a fixed-effect with a
random-effects model, or a consistency with an inconsistency model. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The name "effective number of parameters" for $p_D$ is justified by the following identity, which shows
$p_D$ counts parameters when the prior is uninformative and counts fewer when the prior or a hierarchical
structure shrinks them.

::: {#prp-dic-pd}
## The effective number of parameters
Suppose the deviance is quadratic in $\boldsymbol\xi$ near its minimizer $\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$,
$D(\boldsymbol\xi)=(\boldsymbol\xi-\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top\mathcal
I(\boldsymbol\xi-\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})+c$ for a constant $c$ and a positive definite matrix $\mathcal I$,
as holds for a normal likelihood with known variance and, asymptotically, for a regular model with
$\mathcal I$ the Fisher information. Then
$$
p_D=\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(\mathcal I\,\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\bigr).
$$ {#eq-nma-pd-trace}
If in addition the prior is flat, so that the posterior is approximately $\mathcal N(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi},
\mathcal I^{-1})$, then $p_D\approx\operatorname{tr}(I)=\dim\boldsymbol\xi$.
:::

::: {.proof}
We use the quadratic-form expectation identity: for a random vector $\mathbf z$ with mean
$\boldsymbol\nu$ and covariance $\boldsymbol\Sigma$, and a fixed symmetric matrix $M$,
$$
\mathbb E[(\mathbf z-\mathbf a)^\top M(\mathbf z-\mathbf a)]
=\operatorname{tr}(M\boldsymbol\Sigma)+(\boldsymbol\nu-\mathbf a)^\top M(\boldsymbol\nu-\mathbf a),
$$ {#eq-nma-quadform}
which follows by writing $\mathbf z-\mathbf a=(\mathbf z-\boldsymbol\nu)+(\boldsymbol\nu-\mathbf a)$,
expanding, using $\mathbb E[\mathbf z-\boldsymbol\nu]=\mathbf 0$ to kill the cross term, and
$\mathbb E[(\mathbf z-\boldsymbol\nu)^\top M(\mathbf z-\boldsymbol\nu)]
=\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(M(\mathbf z-\boldsymbol\nu)(\mathbf z-\boldsymbol\nu)^\top)
=\operatorname{tr}(M\boldsymbol\Sigma)$ by the cyclic property of trace (@lem-trace-cyclic). Apply
@eq-nma-quadform with $\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y$, mean $\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}$, covariance
$\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)$, matrix $M=\mathcal I$, and $\mathbf
a=\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}$:
$$
\bar D-c=\mathbb E[(\boldsymbol\xi-\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top\mathcal
I(\boldsymbol\xi-\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})\mid\mathbf y]
=\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(\mathcal I\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\bigr)
+(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}-\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top\mathcal I(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}-\hat{\boldsymbol\xi}).
$$
Also $D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})-c=(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}-\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})^\top\mathcal
I(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi}-\hat{\boldsymbol\xi})$. Subtracting,
$p_D=\bar D-D(\bar{\boldsymbol\xi})=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf
y))$, which is @eq-nma-pd-trace. Under a flat prior the Bernstein-von Mises approximation makes the
posterior $\mathcal N(\hat{\boldsymbol\xi},\mathcal I^{-1})$ (@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality,
@thm-conjugate-normal), so $\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\xi\mid\mathbf y)\approx\mathcal I^{-1}$ and
$p_D\approx\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I\mathcal I^{-1})=\operatorname{tr}(I)=\dim\boldsymbol\xi$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why $p_D$ is "effective."** In a hierarchical random-effects network (@def-random-effects), the
study-level effects $\delta_{j,t_{j,1}k}$ are shrunk toward the network contrasts by the heterogeneity
prior, so their posterior variance is smaller than the flat-prior $\mathcal I^{-1}$ and
$p_D<\dim\boldsymbol\xi$. The criterion thus charges a fixed-effect contrast close to one parameter and a
heavily shrunk random effect close to zero, and DIC @eq-nma-dic rewards a random-effects model only when
the extra flexibility improves $\bar D$ by more than the $p_D$ it costs. This is the mechanism by which
DIC adjudicates fixed against random effects, and consistency against inconsistency, in applied network
meta-analysis. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## A worked triangle-plus-extra-arm network {#sec-nma-example}

We now complete the running example of @exm-nma-running, carrying a full fixed-effect analysis of its
network from the design matrix to fitted contrasts, standard errors, a node-split, and a residual
deviance, so that every number can be checked by hand. The network is a triangle of two-arm trials closed
by a single three-arm trial: the "extra arm" that creates a multi-arm correlation block.

::: {#exm-nma-triangle}
## A three-treatment network with one multi-arm trial
The three treatments are those of @exm-nma-running: $1$ = placebo (reference), $2$ = Drug A, and $3$ =
Drug B. Four studies report log odds-ratio contrasts on the logit scale, with arm precisions equal within
each study so that multi-arm contrast estimates carry the correlation $\tfrac12$ of
@thm-re-nma-correlation.

| Study | Arms | Contrast(s) reported | Estimate | Variance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\{1,2\}$ | $\hat d_{12}$ | $0.5$ | $0.10$ |
| 2 | $\{1,3\}$ | $\hat d_{13}$ | $1.0$ | $0.10$ |
| 3 | $\{2,3\}$ | $\hat d_{23}$ | $0.1$ | $0.20$ |
| 4 | $\{1,2,3\}$ | $\hat d_{12},\ \hat d_{13}$ | $0.6,\ 0.9$ | $0.20$ each, covariance $0.10$ |

The treatment-comparison graph $G$ has vertices $\{1,2,3\}$ and edges $12,13,23$ from studies 1, 2, 3
and a further $12,13$ from study 4; it is connected, with $K=3$, $J=4$, $N=2+2+2+3=9$ arms and
$C=N-J=5$ within-study contrasts.

**Step 1: the contrast-based design.** Eliminating the four per-study baselines leaves the five
within-study contrasts as data $\mathbf y=(0.5,1.0,0.1,0.6,0.9)^\top$, with network-contrast parameters
$\mathbf d=(d_2,d_3)^\top$ and design rows from @eq-nma-rt,
$$
\mathbf X=\begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&1\\ -1&1\\ 1&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix},
$$
one row per within-study contrast. Labeling the rows makes the design transparent:

| Row | Study | Contrast | Design row $(d_2,d_3)$ | Data $y$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | $d_{12}=d_2$ | $(1,\ 0)$ | $0.5$ |
| 2 | 2 | $d_{13}=d_3$ | $(0,\ 1)$ | $1.0$ |
| 3 | 3 | $d_{23}=d_3-d_2$ | $(-1,\ 1)$ | $0.1$ |
| 4 | 4 | $d_{12}=d_2$ | $(1,\ 0)$ | $0.6$ |
| 5 | 4 | $d_{13}=d_3$ | $(0,\ 1)$ | $0.9$ |

The contrast incidence rank is $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X)=2=K-1$, so by
@thm-fe-nma-identifiability the contrasts are identifiable.

**Step 2: the covariance matrix.** The first three contrasts come from separate studies and from each
other are independent; the last two come from study 4 and share its baseline arm, so by the equal-precision
remark after @thm-re-nma-correlation they have correlation $\tfrac12$. Thus
$\boldsymbol\Sigma=\operatorname{blockdiag}(0.10,\,0.10,\,0.20,\,\boldsymbol\Sigma_4)$ with
$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma_4=\begin{pmatrix}0.20&0.10\\0.10&0.20\end{pmatrix}=0.10\,(I_2+J_2),
\qquad
\boldsymbol\Sigma_4^{-1}=\frac{10}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix},
$$
since $(I_2+J_2)^{-1}=\tfrac13\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and the off-diagonal correlation is
$0.10/0.20=\tfrac12$.

**Step 3: the weighted normal equations.** The precision is $10$ for contrasts 1 and 2, $5$ for contrast
3, and the block $\boldsymbol\Sigma_4^{-1}$ for contrasts 4 and 5. Accumulating
$\mathbf A=\mathbf X^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf X$ and $\mathbf b=\mathbf
X^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf y$ row by row, the independent contrasts contribute
$$
10\!\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}
+10\!\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
+5\!\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}15&-5\\-5&15\end{pmatrix},
$$
while study 4, whose two rows form the identity, contributes its precision block
$\boldsymbol\Sigma_4^{-1}=\tfrac{10}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Hence
$$
\mathbf A=\begin{pmatrix}15&-5\\-5&15\end{pmatrix}+\frac{10}{3}\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}
=\frac{1}{3}\begin{pmatrix}65&-25\\-25&65\end{pmatrix},
\qquad \det\mathbf A=\frac{65^2-25^2}{9}=400.
$$
For the right-hand side, the independent contrasts give $10(0.5)\binom{1}{0}+10(1.0)\binom{0}{1}
+5(0.1)\binom{-1}{1}=\binom{4.5}{10.5}$, and study 4 gives
$\boldsymbol\Sigma_4^{-1}\binom{0.6}{0.9}=\tfrac{10}{3}\binom{2(0.6)-0.9}{-0.6+2(0.9)}
=\tfrac{10}{3}\binom{0.3}{1.2}=\binom{1}{4}$, so
$$
\mathbf b=\binom{4.5}{10.5}+\binom{1}{4}=\binom{5.5}{14.5}.
$$

**Step 4: fitted contrasts and standard errors.** Inverting,
$$
\mathbf A^{-1}=\frac{1}{1200}\begin{pmatrix}65&25\\25&65\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf d}=\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf b
=\frac{1}{1200}\begin{pmatrix}65&25\\25&65\end{pmatrix}\binom{5.5}{14.5}
=\frac{1}{1200}\binom{720}{1080}=\binom{0.60}{0.90}.
$$
So $\hat d_2=0.60$ and $\hat d_3=0.90$, each with variance $65/1200=0.054167$ and standard error
$0.2327$, and with covariance $25/1200=0.020833$. The derived contrast is
$\hat d_{23}=\hat d_3-\hat d_2=0.30$, with variance
$(65+65-2\cdot25)/1200=80/1200=0.066667$ and standard error $0.2582$.

**Step 5: node-split of the $2$ versus $3$ comparison.** The direct evidence on $d_{23}$ is study 3
alone, $\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{23}=0.1$ with variance $0.20$. The indirect evidence is the network
refitted without study 3, that is, studies 1, 2, 4. Repeating Steps 3 and 4 with the third contrast
dropped gives
$$
\mathbf A_{\mathrm{ind}}=\frac13\begin{pmatrix}50&-10\\-10&50\end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathbf A_{\mathrm{ind}}^{-1}=\frac{1}{800}\begin{pmatrix}50&10\\10&50\end{pmatrix},\quad
\mathbf b_{\mathrm{ind}}=\binom{6}{14},\quad
\hat{\mathbf d}_{\mathrm{ind}}=\binom{0.55}{0.95},
$$
so the indirect estimate is $\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{23}=0.95-0.55=0.40$, with variance
$(50+50-2\cdot10)/800=80/800=0.10$. The inconsistency statistic is
$$
\hat\omega_{23}=\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{23}-\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{23}=0.1-0.4=-0.30,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\hat\omega_{23})=0.20+0.10=0.30,
$$
by @prp-node-split-test, giving $\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}=0.5477$ and
$z=-0.30/0.5477=-0.55$, a two-sided $p$-value of about $0.58$: no evidence of inconsistency, though the
test is underpowered, as the large standard error warns. As a check on @prp-network-contrast-pooling, the
inverse-variance blend of direct ($0.1$, precision $5$) and indirect ($0.4$, precision $10$) is
$(5\cdot0.1+10\cdot0.4)/15=4.5/15=0.30$, exactly the full-network $\hat d_{23}$ of Step 4.

**Step 6: residual deviance.** The fitted contrasts are $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=\mathbf X\hat{\mathbf
d}$: for the five data rows, $\hat\theta=(0.60,\,0.90,\,0.30,\,0.60,\,0.90)$. Laying the fit beside the
data row by row,

| Row | Study | Contrast | Observed $y$ | Fitted $\hat\theta$ | Residual $r$ | Variance | Deviance contribution |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | $d_{12}$ | $0.5$ | $0.60$ | $-0.10$ | $0.10$ | $0.10$ |
| 2 | 2 | $d_{13}$ | $1.0$ | $0.90$ | $0.10$ | $0.10$ | $0.10$ |
| 3 | 3 | $d_{23}$ | $0.1$ | $0.30$ | $-0.20$ | $0.20$ | $0.20$ |
| 4 | 4 | $d_{12}$ | $0.6$ | $0.60$ | $0$ | $0.20$ | $0$ |
| 5 | 4 | $d_{13}$ | $0.9$ | $0.90$ | $0$ | $0.20$ | $0$ |

The residuals are $\mathbf r=\mathbf y-\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=(-0.10,\,0.10,\,-0.20,\,0,\,0)$, and for a
normal likelihood the residual deviance is the quadratic form
$D_{\mathrm{res}}=\mathbf r^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf r$. Because the two study-$4$ residuals are
zero, that correlated block contributes nothing (in general it would contribute
$\mathbf r_4^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma_4^{-1}\mathbf r_4$, not a sum of separate squares), and
$$
D_{\mathrm{res}}=\frac{(-0.10)^2}{0.10}+\frac{(0.10)^2}{0.10}+\frac{(-0.20)^2}{0.20}+0
=0.1+0.1+0.2=0.40 .
$$

*Degrees of freedom.* We fit $p=2$ parameters $(d_2,d_3)$ to $N_{\mathrm{obs}}=5$ contrast data points, so
the residual degrees of freedom are $5-2=3$. This agrees with the arm-level count of
@def-residual-deviance: the network has $N=9$ arms and, in the reference-treatment parameterization,
$J+K-1=4+2=6$ free parameters (four baselines and two contrasts), giving $9-6=3$ as well. The two counts
match because profiling out the four baselines, that is, eliminating them from the likelihood so that only
the contrasts remain (the concentration step of @sec-nma-glm), converts $9$ arms into $5$ contrasts and
$6$ parameters into $2$; the residual degrees of freedom are unchanged. Since $D_{\mathrm{res}}=0.40$ sits well below its
reference value $3$, the model fits excellently, consistent with the small node-split statistic of Step 5.

*Why the study-$4$ rows fit exactly.* The zero residuals on rows $4$ and $5$ are a feature of these
particular numbers, not a general phenomenon. Studies $1$, $2$, $3$ alone already imply
$(\hat d_2,\hat d_3)=(0.60,0.90)$ (solve the top-left contribution
$\begin{pmatrix}15&-5\\-5&15\end{pmatrix}\hat{\mathbf d}=\binom{4.5}{10.5}$), and study $4$ happens to
report exactly $(0.6,0.9)$, so it agrees perfectly and adds nothing to the residuals. With generic data the
two evidence streams would disagree slightly and all five residuals would be nonzero; read no structural
meaning into the exact fit.

**Clinical reading.** On the log-odds scale the pooled estimates are $\hat d_2=0.60$ for Drug A versus
placebo and $\hat d_3=0.90$ for Drug B versus placebo, that is, odds ratios $e^{0.60}\approx1.82$ and
$e^{0.90}\approx2.46$: both drugs raise the odds of a good outcome, Drug B more so. The head-to-head
contrast is $\hat d_{23}=\hat d_3-\hat d_2=0.30$, an odds ratio $e^{0.30}\approx1.35$ favoring Drug B over
Drug A. Its standard error $0.258$ gives a rough $95\%$ interval $0.30\pm1.96(0.258)=(-0.21,\,0.81)$ on the
log-odds scale, an odds-ratio interval of about $(0.81,\,2.24)$; because this interval includes $1$, the
network does not establish that Drug B beats Drug A, even though the point estimate leans that way. This is
the everyday output of an NMA: a coherent set of relative effects, each with an interval, that a decision
maker can compare on one scale. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the example exhibits.** Every structural feature of the chapter appears in the arithmetic. The
design matrix $\mathbf X$ is the contrast incidence of @eq-nma-design with the baselines profiled out; its
rank $2=K-1$ is the identifiability condition of @thm-fe-nma-identifiability. The block
$\boldsymbol\Sigma_4=0.10(I_2+J_2)$ is the one-half-correlation structure of @thm-re-nma-correlation,
here in its sampling-covariance guise; treating study 4 as two independent trials would have used the
wrong weights. The estimator @eq-nma-gls is the generalized least squares solution
$\hat{\mathbf d}=\mathbf A^{-1}\mathbf b$. The node-split of Step 5 instantiates @def-node-splitting and
@prp-node-split-test, and the pooling identity of @prp-network-contrast-pooling is confirmed to four
figures. The residual deviance of Step 6 is the normal-likelihood form of @def-residual-deviance, with
the correlated block handled by the quadratic form $\mathbf r^\top\boldsymbol\Sigma^{-1}\mathbf r$ rather
than a sum of independent squares. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## Notes and references {#sec-nma-notes}

The network meta-analysis model in its arm-based and contrast-based forms, the two parameterizations of
@def-baseline-shift-param and @def-reference-treatment-param, the consistency equations, the random-effects
covariance with its one-half correlation, residual deviance, and the deviance information criterion are
the standard apparatus of the field as codified by @dias2018nma and the thesis of @phillippo2019thesis,
building on the indirect comparison of @bucher1997 (Chapter 14) and the random-effects meta-analysis of
@dersimonian1986 (Chapter 13). The reference-treatment decomposition @eq-nma-rt is Eq. (1.7c) of
@phillippo2019thesis; the corrected statement of the parameterization equivalence
(@thm-parameterization-equivalence), as an isomorphism onto the consistency-constrained subspace rather
than a square change of basis, follows the proof catalogue's amendment to that footnote, and is needed
precisely because multi-arm trials and repeated comparisons make the baseline-shift count $N$ exceed the
reference-treatment count $J+K-1$.

The identifiability theorem (@thm-fe-nma-identifiability) is folklore in the NMA literature, usually
stated as "the network must be connected"; the formulation here as the rank of the design matrix, reduced
to the rank of a graph incidence matrix (@lem-incidence-rank), makes it a theorem of algebraic graph
theory. The incidence-rank result $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf B)=K-q$ is classical and may be found in
standard texts on algebraic graph theory; the elementary kernel proof given here uses only rank-nullity
and the linear algebra of Chapter 1 (@thm-rank-nullity, @lem-injective-trivial-kernel) and the
positive-definite machinery of Chapter 3 (@thm-pd-characterization, @prp-matrix-square-root), and is
self-contained. The reduction of generalized least squares to ordinary least squares by whitening, used
in @thm-fe-nma-identifiability, is Aitken's theorem, here routed through the Gauss-Markov theorem
(@thm-ols-blue) of Chapter 6.

The one-half contrast correlation (@thm-re-nma-correlation) is the homoscedastic multi-arm covariance of
Lu and Ades; the symmetry characterization (@lem-half-correlation-forced), that one half is the unique
correlation making the heterogeneity variance independent of the baseline choice, sharpens the usual
presentation, which exhibits the value without showing it is forced. Node-splitting (@def-node-splitting,
@prp-node-split-test) is due to Dias and colleagues and is presented in @dias2018nma; the framing as a
released consistency equation, and the connection to the inverse-variance blend
(@prp-network-contrast-pooling), make the test's mean-zero null and its power limitations transparent. The
deviance information criterion (@def-dic, @prp-dic-pd) is due to Spiegelhalter and colleagues; the
trace identity for $p_D$ is standard, and its use for model comparison in network meta-analysis is
described in @dias2018nma. The individual-patient-data network meta-regression
(@thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability) and its dependence on shared effect modifiers, connectedness, and
within-study covariate variation is the foundation of the multilevel network meta-regression of
@phillippo2020mlnmr and is discussed in the indirect-comparison guidance of @phillippo2016tsd18.

This chapter corresponds to results D.5 (baseline-shift), D.6 (reference-treatment), D.7 (equivalence),
D.8 (fixed-effect identifiability), D.9 (one-half correlation), D.10 (consistency closure), D.11
(node-splitting), D.12 (IPD network meta-regression), D.13 (residual deviance), and D.14 (DIC) of the
proof catalogue in `proofs/D_network_meta_analysis.md`. The companion Coq development formalizes only the
Bucher algebra (results D.2 and D.3) in `theories/Bucher.v`, which underwrites the node-split null of
@prp-node-split-test through @thm-bucher-unbiased and @thm-bucher-variance; the network-level results of
this chapter, being linear-algebra and likelihood arguments over the incidence matrix and the design
matrix, are not currently in the Coq tree, and carry no machine-checked tag. The breakdown of consistency
under effect modification, where a significant node-split comes from, is the subject of Chapter 16
(@thm-failure-of-bucher, @def-ecological-bias); the extension of the IPD model to mixed
individual-and-aggregate networks is the multilevel network meta-regression of Part V.

## Exercises {#sec-nma-exercises}

Exercises marked with a star ($\star$) have a full solution in Appendix F. The first two are warm-ups:
draw the picture and read the signs before turning to the computations and proofs.

::: {#exr-nma-draw}
**(Warm-up.) Draw the network and name its parts.** Using the four trials of @exm-nma-running (placebo
$=1$, Drug A $=2$, Drug B $=3$), draw the treatment-comparison graph. (a) For each of the three treatment
pairs, state whether the network has direct evidence, indirect evidence, or both. (b) Is the graph
connected? Name a path from Drug A to Drug B that does not use the direct head-to-head trial. (c) Identify
the loop, and state in words the consistency equation it imposes on $d_{12}$, $d_{13}$, $d_{23}$. (d) If
study $3$ (the head-to-head trial) were removed, would the network still be connected, and would any
inconsistency remain testable?
:::

::: {#exr-nma-sign}
**(Warm-up, interpretation.) Reading contrasts as odds ratios.** On the log-odds scale a network reports
$d_{12}=0.5$ (Drug A versus placebo) and $d_{13}=1.0$ (Drug B versus placebo). (a) Convert each to an odds
ratio. (b) Under consistency (@thm-consistency-closure), what is $d_{23}$, the Drug B versus Drug A
contrast, and its odds ratio? (c) Write the same comparison in the reverse direction, $d_{32}$, as a
log-odds contrast and an odds ratio. (d) A colleague reports "the odds ratio for treatment $2$ versus
treatment $3$ is $0.61$." Is this consistent with your answer, and why is naming the direction essential?
:::

::: {#exr-nma-design}
**From a network to a design matrix.** A network has four treatments $1,2,3,4$ ($1$ the reference) and
three two-arm studies: study A on $\{1,2\}$, study B on $\{2,3\}$, study C on $\{3,4\}$. Write the
treatment-comparison graph, the signed incidence matrix $\mathbf B$, and the reference-treatment contrast
design $\mathbf X_d$. Compute $\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf B)$ from @lem-incidence-rank and confirm the
network is connected and the three contrasts $d_2,d_3,d_4$ are identifiable. Which pairwise contrasts have
only indirect evidence?
:::

::: {#exr-nma-incidence}
**Disconnection and non-identifiability.** Remove study B from the previous network, leaving studies A
on $\{1,2\}$ and C on $\{3,4\}$. Show the graph has two components, compute
$\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}})$ from @thm-fe-nma-identifiability, and exhibit an explicit
nonzero vector in the kernel of $\mathbf X_{\mathrm{RT}}$. Which contrasts become non-identifiable, and
which remain identifiable?
:::

::: {#exr-nma-threearm-cov}
**A four-arm covariance.** Using @thm-re-nma-correlation, write the $3\times3$ heterogeneity covariance
matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma_j$ of the three baseline contrasts of a four-arm trial. Verify its eigenvalues
are $2\tau^2$ once and $\tfrac{\tau^2}{2}$ twice, and that $\det\boldsymbol\Sigma_j=4(\tau^2/2)^3$.
Confirm directly that the variance of the derived contrast $\delta_{j,kl}=\delta_{j,1l}-\delta_{j,1k}$
equals $\tau^2$, consistent with @lem-half-correlation-forced.
:::

::: {#exr-nma-closure-count}
**Counting loop constraints.** For a network with $K=5$ treatments, use @thm-consistency-closure to find
the number of basis contrasts and the number of independent consistency (loop) constraints among the
$\binom{5}{2}$ pairwise contrasts. Verify the count two ways: by the formula $\binom{K-1}{2}$ and by the
cycle rank $|\mathcal E|-K+1$ of the complete graph $K_5$.
:::

::: {#exr-nma-dic}
**Effective parameters under shrinkage.** Consider a one-parameter normal model
$y\sim\mathcal N(\theta,\sigma^2)$ with known $\sigma^2$ and a conjugate prior
$\theta\sim\mathcal N(0,\kappa^2)$. Using the conjugate posterior (@thm-conjugate-normal) and
@prp-dic-pd, compute $p_D=\mathcal I\operatorname{Var}(\theta\mid y)$ with $\mathcal I=1/\sigma^2$, and
show $p_D=\kappa^2/(\kappa^2+\sigma^2)\in(0,1)$. Confirm $p_D\to 1$ as $\kappa^2\to\infty$ (flat prior)
and $p_D\to 0$ as $\kappa^2\to 0$ (point-mass prior), so a shrunk parameter counts as less than one.
:::

::: {#exr-nma-recompute}
**Recompute the worked example with a discrepant direct study.** In @exm-nma-triangle, replace the study
3 estimate $\hat d_{23}=0.1$ by $\hat d_{23}=1.0$, keeping its variance $0.20$ and all other data
unchanged. Recompute the full-network $\hat d_2,\hat d_3$, the node-split statistic $\hat\omega_{23}$ and
its standard error, and the residual deviance. Comment on whether the inconsistency is now detectable and
how the residual deviance reflects it.
:::

::: {#exr-nma-pooling}
**($\star$) The network estimate is the direct-indirect blend.** Prove @prp-network-contrast-pooling from the
generalized least squares estimator @eq-nma-gls in the special case of a contrast informed by exactly two
independent sources. That is, take a $2\times1$ design $\mathbf X=\binom{1}{1}$ with diagonal covariance
$\operatorname{diag}(v_{\mathrm{dir}},v_{\mathrm{ind}})$ and data
$(\hat d^{\mathrm{dir}}_{AB},\hat d^{\mathrm{ind}}_{AB})$, and show @eq-nma-gls reduces to the
inverse-variance-weighted mean @eq-nma-pooling with variance $1/(w_{\mathrm{dir}}+w_{\mathrm{ind}})$.
Then explain why, in a larger network, the same blend holds for any contrast whose only evidence splits
into one direct and one indirect independent stream, and relate this to the node-split of
@def-node-splitting.
:::

::: {#exr-nma-ipd-collinear}
**($\star$) An unidentifiable network meta-regression.** In the IPD network meta-regression @eq-nma-ipdnmr with
a single scalar covariate $x$, suppose $x$ is constant within each study (it varies only between studies).
Show that condition (iii) of @thm-ipd-nmr-identifiability fails and that the prognostic main effect
$\beta_1$ is confounded with the study baselines $\mu_j$: exhibit a one-parameter family of distinct
parameter vectors $(\boldsymbol\mu,\beta_1,\dots)$ that give identical conditional means on all arms.
Explain in one or two sentences why this is the individual-level seed of ecological bias
(@def-ecological-bias), and why within-study covariate variation rescues identifiability.
:::
